problem: Right-click never reaches attack2. The button name is built from the raw DOM index — `input.press(`Mouse${event.button}`)` — but MouseEvent.button is 0=left, 1=MIDDLE, 2=RIGHT. attack2 is bound to ['Mouse1'] (line 70), so the right button presses the unbound "Mouse2" and does nothing, while the middle/wheel button fires attack2. Verified empirically against a live headless world: button=2 -> press("Mouse2") -> attack=false attack2=false; button=1 -> attack2=true. This directly breaks spec item 5 ("Bind attack2 to Mouse1. Suppress the context menu on the canvas so right-click aims") and the file's own comment at line 297 ("Right-click aims down the sights"). The context menu is suppressed, so right-click in play mode is silently dead. Needs an explicit map, e.g. {0:'Mouse0', 2:'Mouse1'}, not the DOM index.

The stuck-button guard misses the button most likely to be held. On unlock only 'Mouse0' and 'Mouse1' are released, but the right button pressed at line 272 is named 'Mouse2', so a right button held when Escape returns the pointer stays in the keyboard plugin's `down` set forever — no mouseup ever arrives, and `blur` only fires if the window loses focus. This is exactly the failure the comment on lines 252-254 claims to prevent. Same root cause as the mapping bug; both are fixed by mapping the button index once.

`wanted < 0` accepts zero, so a sensitivity of 0 is stored and the mouse is silently dead. Verified: `node bin/engine.mjs --headless run mouse.sensitivity 0` exits 0 and returns {"sensitivity":0,"degreesPerCount":0,"radiansPerCount":0} — a mouse that cannot turn the view, reported as success, which is the exact silent failure the plugin's own error text ("must be a positive number") says it refuses. `Number('')` is also 0, so an empty argument disables looking with no message. Should be `wanted <= 0`.

The test cannot catch the button-mapping bug it is meant to cover. It presses the code string directly (`input.press('Mouse1')`) and asserts `held('attack2')`, which only re-tests `bind` — the mousedown handler that derives 'Mouse1' from event.button is never exercised, so the test passes green while right-click is broken in the browser. The signs are testable headless because `lookFromMouse` was extracted as a pure function; the button mapping deserves the same treatment (export the index->name map and assert map[2] === 'Mouse1').

`accumulated.wheel += event.deltaY` stores the raw delta and ignores `event.deltaMode`. One notch is ~100-120 (DOM_DELTA_PIXEL, Chrome), ~3 (DOM_DELTA_LINE, Firefox default) or ~1 (DOM_DELTA_PAGE), so any threshold the weapon-switching agent picks against `mouseWheel()` will be right in one browser and wrong in another. Neither the units nor deltaMode are normalised or documented on the accessor.

Clicks during play still reach the editor's transform tool. mouse-look listens for `mousedown` on the canvas, but tool-transform listens for `pointerdown` on the parent viewport (plugins/builtin/tool-transform.js:202) with no `loop.running` guard, and pointerdown fires before mousedown so preventDefault here cannot stop it. Every shot fired in play mode therefore also runs `renderer.pick`, changes `editor.selection`, emits selection:changed and repaints every panel. Damage is transient (clientX is frozen under pointer lock so the 'move' drag resolves to zero, and the level reloads on stop), but the editor churns on every trigger pull. Fixable inside the owned file with a capture-phase pointerdown listener that stopPropagation()s while `input.locked`.

Documented deviation, confirmed real: `jump` is rebound to ['Space','ArrowUp'], dropping KeyW, against the spec's "Do not disturb the existing left/right/up/down/jump/fire bindings". The reasoning is sound and the blast radius is small — project/types/player.js only reads held('jump'), project/tests/jump.js presses codes('jump')[0] === 'Space', KeyW survives on `up`, and no doc anywhere in the repo mentions KeyW — but W no longer jumps for a human playing the 2D demo, and the change is locked in by an assertion (project/tests/mouse-look.js:77) so it will outlive the reason for it.

`world.look` from the CLI reports the DEFAULTS, never the level's world block — the exact acceptance check in the spec, answering wrongly. The `level:loaded` listener is `async` and `bus.emit` does not await it, so `await context.files.read(...)` is still pending when the command runs. Verified: `node bin/engine.mjs --headless --level de_dust2 run world.look` returns {"declared":{},"sky":null,"skyTexture":null,"fog":{"density":0}} and the note `the level declares no "world" block, so these are the defaults`, while project/levels/de_dust2.json:8-22 declares all five keys (sky #a8b8c8, skyTexture, fog [0.012,#c3bda8], ambient, sun). Waiting 300ms in-process and calling report() again returns the correct block, which pins it as the race. An agent asking "why is this level dark" is told, confidently and in prose, that the level said nothing. The raw level is already sitting in memory in engine/start-world.js:190 (`loadedLevel`), so the async re-read is what creates the window.

`world.set` cannot turn fog on for a level that declares no fog, and says nothing about it. `readFog(null)` returns `{ density: 0 }` — every other reader returns `{}` for a missing value — and `parts()` at line 197 spreads the DECLARED reading first, so that 0 overwrites the DEFAULT_FOG_DENSITY laid down at line 209 before the override is merged. Verified: `run world.set '["fog","#c3bda8"]'` -> {"density":0,"color":"#c3bda8"}; `run world.set '["fog",true]'` -> {"density":0}. No note, no error, no console line — the fog you just asked for is simply off. The agent's own summary claims "0.014 only fills in for 'fog': true or a colour-only fog"; that holds for a declared block (verified: declared `"fog":"#c3bda8"` -> 0.014) but is false for the world.set path, which is the path the command exists for.

The documented skyTexture path 404s, so the sky box — the headline feature — never appears. buildSkyBox passes the name through `assetURL` (engine/ui.js:21-24), which maps any string containing a slash to `/project/<name>`. So the example in this file's own header (line 11) and in project/levels/de_dust2.json:10, `"counter-strike/sky.png"`, resolves to `/project/counter-strike/sky.png`. The file is at `project/assets/counter-strike/sky.png` (verified with fs.existsSync); the string that actually resolves is `assets/counter-strike/sky.png`. It degrades gracefully and names itself in the console, so this is not a crash — but the sky box is untested against a real asset and does not work with the only value anyone will copy. Note the same broken convention is used by de_dust2.json's mesh textures and by the spec's own example, so it is not solely this agent's doing.

The sky sphere maps a half-sky backdrop over a full sphere, so the horizon band ends up under the floor. The shipped project/assets/counter-strike/sky.png is 256x256 and is authored zenith->horizon and tiling ACROSS only (tools/make-counter-strike-textures.mjs:1390 `wrap: 'x'`, and its comment at :1193-1195), i.e. a cylindrical band, not an equirectangular panorama. Over SphereGeometry, V spans 180 degrees, so the pale `horizon` colour (#d5cfbe, image bottom) lands at the nadir and the cool `middle` (#8ea5bb) sits at the actual horizon — the opposite of the "fog matched to the sky so the two agree at the horizon" argument at lines 205-207. U spans 360 degrees, so 256px is stretched around the whole sky; `texture.wrapS = RepeatWrapping` at line 366 has no effect because repeat is left at (1,1). BackSide alone also mirrors the image east-west relative to the sun direction.

A sky texture that fails to load can never be retried. `look.skyFile = wanted` is assigned at line 320 BEFORE the load starts, and the `.catch` at line 342 leaves it assigned, so re-issuing the same value — a level reload, or `world.set '["skyTexture", "..."]'` — hits the `wanted === look.skyFile` early return at line 319 and does nothing. Combined with the 404 above, the only way back is to set a different string first.

The frame system's "put the sky back" guard does not survive a replaced scene. `if (!sky.parent) context.renderer?.scene?.add(sky)` only fires when the mesh was removed from its parent; if a renderer rewrite constructs a NEW THREE.Scene, `sky.parent` still points at the old one and the guard never fires. The claim that "a renderer rewrite cannot make the sky silently vanish" is overstated — it covers scene.clear()/remove() only.

`report()` states values that were not applied. `drive()` returns a boolean at lines 289/293/297 and all four call sites (90-93) discard it, and `notes()` (428-438) has no case for a missing or throwing setter. Verified with a stub renderer lacking setFog: the console got one `[World Look] this renderer has no setFog()` line and the other three setters still ran (that part of the claim holds), but `world.look` still printed the fog density as if it were live. The message does reach the engine log ring via console.error, so it is not wholly silent — but the one report whose stated purpose is answering "why is this level dark" does not mention it.

The colour check accepts values the renderer then rejects, which is the failure this function's own comment says it exists to prevent. `/^[a-z]+$/i` passes any bare word (`purpleish`), and the hex branch accepts 4- and 8-digit forms that engine/render.js:72 (`HEX`, 3 or 6 digits only) refuses. render.js then logs and `setSky` assigns `scene.background = null` (render.js:593-597) — no sky at all — while `world.look` continues to report the colour as set.

right() is only ever evaluated at yaw 0, where both signs it could get wrong are zero. `test.near(beside.z, 0, 1e-9, 'right at yaw 0 has no Z')` is satisfied by -sin(yaw) AND by +sin(yaw) alike, and right() is never called at a non-zero yaw anywhere in the file. The brief singles out this exact function ('a sign error here means the game shoots backwards'), and the agent's notes claim it is 'verified numerically end to end' — but the committed test would not catch a flipped Z. I confirmed the shipped code is correct (right == forward x up, orthonormal, |right| = 1 at yaw 0.9), so this is a coverage hole rather than a live bug; it leaves the strafe/shoot direction unguarded for the five agents about to build on it. One line at a non-zero yaw fixes it.

The first-person branch returns before the guard that protects the editor's viewport. The 2D path has `if (!cam.target) return` at line 256 with a comment at 254-255 stating the invariant: 'an agent calling simulate() while editing should not find its viewport moved.' Line 251 dispatches to firstPerson() ahead of it, and firstPerson() writes view.yaw/view.pitch unconditionally. Verified on de_dust2 in edit mode: with a pending context.input.lookBy(1.0, 0.3), engine.simulate(0.2) moved the editor view from yaw 0 / pitch 0 to yaw 1.001 / pitch 0.302. Needs a non-empty look accumulator to trigger (pointer lock is refused while not playing, so the realistic caller is a bot or a test), but the comment now asserts an invariant the code no longer enforces for first-person levels.

Recoil only decays while view.mode === 'first-person'. punch() is exposed on context.camera unconditionally, but the decay (`cam.punchYaw = settle(cam.punchYaw * keep)`) lives inside firstPerson(), which the system skips in any other mode. Verified: in ortho, camera.punch(0.5, 0.5) followed by 10 s of stepping leaves punchPitch and punchYaw at exactly 0.5, and camera.state then reports `aim: {yaw: 0.5, pitch: 0.5}` forever on a 2D level. forget() clears it on level load and on play start/stop, so it cannot survive a level change — but within a session a 2D weapon calling punch() poisons aim(), forward() and right() permanently. The spec says decay runs 'on the fixed clock', with no mode qualifier.

The view bob is switched off instantly rather than eased out, so the eye jumps by up to a full bob amplitude in a single step. `const effort = grounded ? Math.min(1, speed / RUN_SPEED) : 0` multiplies the sine directly, so effort goes 1 -> 0 in one step the moment the body stops or leaves the ground, wherever the sine happens to be. Measured with a body nothing else simulates: stopping at a bob extreme moved the eye 0.0349 m (one full BOB_AMPLITUDE) in one 1/60 s step — an instantaneous ~2 m/s vertical camera velocity. The same discontinuity fires on every step off a ledge, when grounded flips to false. The eye height ducking was eased for exactly this reason ('a snap reads as a glitch'); the bob was not.

forward() is never checked for unit length, which the spec explicitly requires ('return unit vectors from yaw and pitch'). Every assertion in the basis block — yaw 0 gives (0,0,-1) at lines 71-73, yaw PI/2 gives x = -1 at line 81, pitch 89 degrees gives y > 0.99 at line 84 — is equally satisfied by the unnormalised `(-sin yaw, sin pitch, -cos yaw)` with the cos(pitch) factor dropped. A dropped cos(pitch) is a classic first-person regression: it leaves the horizontal aim correct and silently lengthens the ray as you look up, which nothing downstream would notice until bullet ranges started disagreeing with the crosshair.

The test never enters play mode, so spec items 1 and 6 have zero coverage. test.simulate() calls loop.step() directly (plugins/builtin/tests.js:223), so play:started and play:stopped never fire; the test sets view.mode = 'first-person' by hand at line 36 instead. That leaves untested: the rule applying view.mode and view.fov on play (item 1), and the restore of mode/fov/yaw/pitch/z on stop (item 6) — the item whose stated failure mode is 'leaving play mode strands the editor inside a perspective camera pointing at a wall'. I verified both work by driving the bus manually on de_dust2 (play set mode first-person / fov 90 / follow player-0; stop restored x 7, y 3, z 0), so the code is right, but the two bus-driven paths have nothing guarding them. Item 5 (bob and landing dip), item 7 (camera.state) and item 8 (angular shake) are likewise asserted nowhere; I verified all three by hand.

camera.state reports the editor's viewport as the player's eye when there is no follow target. With de_dust2 loaded in edit mode the command answers `eye: [7,3,0], eyeHeight: 0, following: null` — eyeHeight 0 reads as 'the eye is on the floor' rather than 'there is no eye', and eye is just view.x/y/z, which in edit mode is wherever the editor is looking. The command's own comment at lines 299-300 claims it answers 'what can the player see right now ... rather than a screenshot'. This is the same honesty argument the agent used to justify awaiting cam.ruleRead so `rule: {}` would not read as 'the level declared no camera'; the null target case was missed. `cam.eyeHeight ?? 0` at line 303 should stay null, and eye should be gated on cam.target rather than on mode alone.

One fixed step of eye lag, disclosed by the agent but worth confirming as real. Plugins load by sorted filename, so camera.js runs its fixed system before physics-2d.js and physics-3d.js, and moveEye reads entity.y at the start of the step. Verified on de_dust2: one step after play, view.y = 2.17 (from the spawn feet at 0.55) while the player had already been moved to y = 0.9939. At a 6.35 m/s run that is ~0.106 m of trailing every frame, and because the read is pre-collision-resolution the frame you are pushed out of a wall renders from inside it. The agent's stated reason for not adding `needs: ['Physics 3D']` — that it would also retime the 2D camera — is sound, but I measured the 2D path as bit-identical to HEAD (max delta exactly 0 over 120 steps with lerp, lookAhead, offsetY and bounds active), so the 2D regression risk of reordering is smaller than the note implies.

BLOCKER, and the agent's report understates it by 16x. The agent said "Three type files currently reference them without the assets/ prefix". In fact de_dust2.json contains 231 texture references across 16 distinct filenames, ALL missing the assets/ prefix (sky, concrete, sand-floor, stairs-stone, tunnel-floor, tunnel-wall, plaster-trim, plaster-wall, sandstone-brick, sandstone-block, ceiling-dark, tarp-blue, roof-tile, metal-panel, door-blue, door-metal). Verified by simulating engine/ui.js assetURL against disk: 'counter-strike/sand-floor.png' -> /project/counter-strike/sand-floor.png -> 404, while 'assets/counter-strike/sand-floor.png' -> EXISTS. Anyone who follows the agent's stated fix ("add the assets/ prefix in those three files") still gets a completely untextured map. skyTexture on this line goes through world-look.js:363 assetURL and will reject with '404 /project/counter-strike/sky.png', falling back to the flat sky colour.

MAJOR, and it is why the above went unnoticed. problemsIn() validates type load errors, behaviour load errors, level JSON validity, missing behaviour attachments and test load errors, but never checks that a referenced texture/sprite/asset file exists on disk. All 231 broken texture references pass `node bin/engine.mjs check` silently (I confirmed: ok:true, problems:[]). The comment at line 234 argues that a missing behaviour attachment 'is silent at runtime except for one console line' and must be caught here; the identical argument applies to a missing texture (render.js:51 logs '[render] missing texture ...') and is not acted on. The texture agent cited this green check as part of its proof, so the proof does not support the claim.

MAJOR (the agent did report these three, and they are still real and unfixed). texture: 'counter-strike/sandstone-block.png' resolves via assetURL to /project/counter-strike/sandstone-block.png and 404s. Same defect at project/types/crate.js:13 ('counter-strike/crate-wood.png') and project/types/door.js:13 ('counter-strike/door-blue.png'). All three need the assets/ prefix.

Sign error: the bullet hole's pit interior is lit on the wrong side. `const lit = clamp01(0.2 - dy / (holeRadius * 6))` makes dy<0 (the TOP of the pit) brighter. Everywhere else this file lights from above and treats protrusions correctly (drawCourses line 302 catches light on the top arris; sandFloor line 356 lights the stone's top and line 360 puts the shadow at centreY+radius; rivets line 975 light the upper-left). A recess lit from above must be DARK at the top-inside and lit at the bottom-inside, i.e. the opposite. Measured on the shipped PNG: pit interior upper half luminance 35.8 vs lower half 28.0 - top is brighter, confirming the inversion. The pale spall ring dominates the read so the decal still passes as a hole, which is why this is minor rather than major, but the internal gradient is backwards and the comment on line 1238 ('the far wall of it catching a little light') describes the wrong wall for overhead light.

Same sign error as line 1239, in concrete's pits: `over(image, centreX + dx, centreY - radius, light, 0.35)` puts the highlight on the UPPER lip, with the comment on line 659 saying 'a dark hole with the light catching its upper lip'. For a recess under overhead light the lit lip is the lower one; as written the shading signature is that of a bump, not a pit. Honest magnitude: I measured 238 pit-core pixels in concrete.png and the brightness 3px above a pit is +0.04 vs the local mean and 3px below is -1.13, so the intended highlight is effectively not deposited at all and the visible result is negligible. Reporting it because the direction is inverted relative to every protrusion in the same file, not because it is currently visible.

The seam self-check runs on the in-memory float surface, not on the file that was just read back off disk. Line 1539 reads the written buffer and lines 1540-1550 decode it, but line 1557 calls seamRatio(image, ...) against the pre-quantisation Float32 surface. The comment at line 1538 ('Read it back off disk rather than trusting what was just built in memory') applies only to the header check. The 8-bit quantisation is what actually ships and is what could introduce a join; the check never looks at it. No live consequence here - my numbers decoded from disk agree with the tool's to within 0.01 - but the agent's summary describes a stronger check than the code performs.

Latent: plaster-trim draws its ground stains with stain(), whose over() wraps in Y via indexOf(), but plaster-trim is declared wrap:'x' and deliberately does NOT tile in Y - it is a composition from the paint edge (y~19) down to the ground. I replayed the seeded RNG for 'plaster-trim' and all three stains wrap past the bottom: centreY 37.8/39.3/38.6 with reach 45/33/30, wrapping back to y=18.8, 8.3 and 4.6, i.e. into and above the clean plaster region. There is no guard. Honest magnitude: the deposit at that radius is in the fade tail, and I measured rows 0-7 of the shipped PNG (means 193.0-193.6, spreads ~15 consistent with the mottle) and could detect no bleed - so it is currently invisible. But a different seed, a lower centre or a larger radius would drop dark ground grime above the paint line, and nothing in the code prevents it.

A texture that 404s only falls back to the visible per-type tint for the FIRST entity that referenced the file. `texture()` registers the onFail callback only on a cache MISS, so every later entity sharing that filename gets `mat.map = base.clone()` of an image-less texture and renders as three.js's 1x1 empty (black) texture with color #ffffff. Verified: four brushes + two sprites all naming 'gone.png', error listeners fired -> w0 and s0 fall back to their tint, w1/w2/w3/s1 keep the broken map at white. On dust2 a mistyped texture name means one correctly-coloured wall and 267 black ones. It contradicts spec item 6 and the file's own comment at lines 405-407 and 449-451. The same shape exists in the baseline sprite path (engine/render.js:404), so it is inherited rather than invented — but the mesh path multiplies the blast radius by ~16x (17 image sources, 268 textured meshes).

`m.material.transparent = opacity < 1` is set without `m.material.needsUpdate = true`, so the mesh never actually dims. three r0.169 puts `transparent` into the program cache key as `parameters.opaque` (WebGLPrograms.js:251, :555) and injects `#define OPAQUE` (WebGLProgram.js:837), which makes opaque_fragment.glsl force `diffuseColor.a = 1.0`. `WebGLRenderer.setProgram` only recompiles when `material.version` changes (WebGLRenderer.js:1837-1944), and I confirmed the version stays 0 across the flip. So the material created opaque keeps `#define OPAQUE` forever: blending turns on, alpha is clamped to 1, nothing visibly changes. This kills the right-click stack-menu hover preview (plugins/builtin/tool-transform.js:191 sets `e.opacity = 0.45`) for every mesh — i.e. exactly in 3D levels, where overlapping-entity disambiguation is the whole point. The agent's own harness asserts 'a dimmed mesh blends' by reading `material.transparent`/`.opacity` (render-harness/run.mjs:156), which passes while the pixels are unchanged.

`behind: p.z > 1` is not the behind-the-eye test the comment and the handover note promise; it is 'outside the depth range'. Measured with camera at (0,1.62,0), yaw 0, fov 90, near 0.05, far 400: a point 401 m DIRECTLY IN FRONT returns `{x:400, y:300, behind:true}` (false positive — a caller told to skip a gizmo that is on screen), and a point 5 m to the side exactly in the eye plane returns `{x:Infinity, y:NaN, behind:false}` (false negative — the caller is told the position is usable and gets Infinity/NaN). A point exactly at the eye gives `{x:NaN, y:NaN, behind:false}`. The correct test is the sign of the view-space w (equivalently, whether the point is in front of the camera plane), not the NDC z.

The `mesh: "wall.png"` shorthand the handover note documents does not apply a texture. `meshShape()` (line 138) handles the string case for SIZE (it falls through to the collider box, verified: a string mesh with `collider.box:[4,3,0.4]` produces a 4x3x0.4 BoxGeometry), but `meshMaterial()` reads `declared.texture` off the string, gets undefined, and returns early with the per-type tint. Verified: `mesh: 'wall.png'` yields `material.map === null`. `look()` (line 185) likewise reads `e.mesh.texture` off the string, so two entities with different string meshes and the same collider share one rebuild key. Nothing in the repo uses the shorthand today, but the handover tells the next agent it works.

`get camera()` returns `activeCamera()` without calling `readyCamera()`, so it hands back the camera as of the last `draw()`/`resize()`/`toScreen()`/`pick()`, not the current `view`. This contradicts the handover's 'the camera currently drawing'. Verified: on a fresh renderer with `view.fov = 60` and a 1024x512 canvas, `renderer.camera` reports fov 90 / aspect 1 / position (0,0,0) before anything has drawn; after moving `view.x`, `view.yaw` and `view.fov` it still reports the previous frame's values. Every other public reader in the file is careful to call `readyCamera()` first (lines 385, 639) — this one is the exception, and it is the one a plugin reaching for `context.renderer.camera` from a pointer handler will hit.

Unreadable geometry and tiling numbers are silently replaced by defaults, while every neighbouring reader in the same file names its failures with a [render] prefix. `number()` uses `Number.isFinite` with no coercion, so `box: ["4","3","0.4"]` becomes a 1x1x1 cube (verified) and `tiling: "2"` or `tiling: NaN` falls back to the default density (verified, repeat 1 instead of 2). Related: `setFog` at line 605 does `Number(density) || 0`, so `setFog('thick', '#ffffff')` turns fog off with no message at all (verified: zero console output for all four cases). Compare `readColour` (line 86), `readIntensity` (line 100) and `aimSun` (line 321), which all report by name — this is the exact silent-failure the file's own header argues against.

`geometryCache` grows without bound and its comment overstates the win. The comment claims 'a map of four hundred walls is a handful of distinct sizes'; the shipped de_dust2.json actually produces 194 distinct BoxGeometries for 281 entities (measured), so the cache saves about 30%, not an order of magnitude. More importantly the key is the exact dimension triple and nothing is ever disposed, so every size ever typed into the inspector — including every intermediate value while someone edits a box dimension — allocates a BoxGeometry that lives for the page. 'Bounded by how many sizes the project actually uses' is only true of a project that is never edited.

NaN velocity silently freezes a body forever, with nothing logged. `let parts = Math.max(1, Math.ceil(travel / smallest))` — Math.max(1, NaN) is NaN, not 1, so the guard does not floor it. `for (let part = 0; part < NaN; part++)` never executes: the body is never moved, never resolved, never grounded, and gravity keeps accumulating on velocityY forever. Verified: set faller.velocityX = NaN, step 60 times — x stays 0, y stays 5, grounded stays false, velocityY reaches -20.32, and `engine.errors()` and `engine.log()` are both empty. The 2D plugin under the same input writes NaN into e.x, so the entity visibly vanishes; here the player just stops, silently. NaN reaches velocity the moment game code normalises a zero-length movement vector, which is the commonest way a shooter produces one. The plugin already has a report() call two lines below for the too-fast case and just misses this one, in a file whose own comment says 'Silence is the enemy'.

canStand fails OPEN for any non-numeric or non-positive height, with no message. `halfHeight: height / 2` is NaN when height is undefined or a string, every comparison in overlap() against NaN is false, and the function returns true. Verified against a real vent that correctly refuses 1.83: canStand(stepper) with the height omitted returns true, canStand(stepper, 'tall') returns true, canStand(stepper, -5) returns true. This is the one function whose entire purpose is to refuse, and a crouch system reading a height off a type that never declared it (`context.canStand(player, player.properties.standHeight)`) gets a confident yes and stands the player up inside the geometry. Nothing is logged, unlike the non-3D-entity path immediately above it, which does report.

asVector silently rewrites a non-finite coordinate to 0, so a bad ray fires from the world origin and returns a confident wrong hit. `{ x: +value[0] || 0, y: +value[1] || 0, z: +value[2] || 0 }` maps NaN, undefined and Infinity all to 0. Verified: ctx.raycast([NaN, 1.5, 2], [1,0,0], 10) returns a hit on `wall` at distance 2.5 — the answer for an origin of x=0, with no indication the origin was garbage. A bare-string origin is correctly named and refused two lines away in castRay, so the surrounding code already knows this input needs naming; the per-component case slips through. On the function the spec calls the single most important one being written, a wrong hit is worse than a null.

options.ignore given a bare id string throws instead of being accepted or refused. `(options.ignore || []).map(...)` — verified: ctx.raycast([0,1.5,0],[1,0,0],10,{ ignore: 'slider' }) throws `TypeError: (options.ignore || []).map is not a function`. This is a likely mistake precisely because the plugin's own physics3d.raycast command accepts a bare id string for `from`, and because 'the shooter skips itself' reads naturally as ignore: entity.id. Either wrap a non-array in one, or name it — a raw TypeError out of the raycast is the least useful of the three outcomes.

The disjoint-domains claim does not hold for the Physics 2D command. The three system filters were guarded with flat(), but `physics.gravity` still writes `properties.gravity` on every entity in the world, and Physics 3D reads exactly that key. Verified: `run physics.gravity -1` on physics-3d-test sets faller.properties.gravity to -1, after which the body falls from y=10 to y=9.49 in a second instead of landing. The 2D plugin's only command silently retunes the 3D world. The spec's guard edit was described as filters only, so this is arguably out of the mandated scope, but the summary's claim that the two plugins 'own disjoint sets of entities with nothing to configure' is not true through this door.

boxFor ignores entity.rotation entirely and says nothing about it. `const [width, height, depth] = entity.collider.box` builds an axis-aligned box from position and scale only; rotation is never read by the mover, the raycast or canStand. Nothing in the 580-line file's otherwise thorough commentary mentions the limitation. No placement in de_dust2 is currently rotated, so this bites nobody today, but the editor's transform tool can rotate one and the `brush` type does not forbid it — the symptom is a wall that is solid in the viewport, walk-through in play, and invisible to every ray, with no warning anywhere.

The surviving test covers the maths but not the contract the other five agents will call. It imports castRay directly from the plugin, so nothing in project/tests exercises context.raycast, context.canStand, the onCollide contact reporting, the trigger rule, sub-stepping or the spatial grid — the wiring the rest of the game depends on has no check that outlives the session. The agent discloses this gap honestly and the five cases the spec demanded are all present and all assert real numbers, so this is not a blocker; I confirmed by hand that both context functions work correctly. Worth recording because the stated reason (a test is handed `test` and never `context`) is a genuine engine limitation that will make every future plugin author reach around the harness the same way.

The shadow cap is spent on lights that physically cannot cast a shadow. `granted = wantsShadow && shadows < SHADOW_CAP` never asks whether the kind supports one. In three 0.169 HemisphereLight and RectAreaLight have no `.shadow` at all (verified: `new THREE.HemisphereLight().shadow === undefined`), only point/spot/directional do. Verified live in a headless world: a hemisphere light with `shadow:true` placed first was GRANTED the single slot, and the spot light behind it — the one that could actually have cast — was refused by name on the console. `lights.report().counts.castingShadows` then answered 1 while nothing casts anything. This defeats the exact promise the file is built around ('one supported well', 'refusals named on the console'): the named warning refuses the working light and grants the broken one. Compounding it, line 609 (`if ('castShadow' in object)`) is always true because castShadow is an Object3D field, so the hemisphere light is pushed into three's shadowsArray and WebGLShadowMap logs 'THREE.WebGLShadowMap: ... has no shadow.' every frame. The test at project/tests/lights.js:108 spawns three lights of the default kind (point) only, so it cannot see this.

No player in this game ever casts or receives a shadow. `markShadowSurfaces` walks `scene.children` and skips anything that is not `object.isMesh`. render.js:1013 `buildModel` returns a `THREE.Group` for any entity declaring `mesh.model`, and project/types/terrorist.js:29, project/types/counter-terrorist.js:23 and project/types/bomb.js:12 all do. So every terrorist, every counter-terrorist and the C4 are Groups and are skipped entirely. A player's shadow thrown round a corner is the single most visible thing a shadow-casting light is for in a shooter, and it is the one case that silently never works. It also never recurses into a merged batch's children or into any nested mesh.

The bake manifest hands the offline baker editor gizmos as geometry to bake. `if (entity.type === 'light' || !entity.mesh) continue` excludes this plugin's own marker box but ignores the engine's existing convention for exactly this — `_definition.marker === true`, read by plugins/builtin/editor-markers.js:33. Verified: `run lights.bake '{"surfaces":true}'` on de_dust2 lists 10 `spawn-point` and 2 `bomb-site` entities among its 280 'static surfaces'. project/types/bomb-site.js declares `mesh.box: [12, 3, 12]`, so the manifest tells Blender there are two solid 12x3x12 metre boxes standing over sites A and B. Baked with those as occluders, both bomb sites come back black. The spec asked for 'an exact manifest'; a one-line `_definition?.marker` test is the fix.

Same root cause in the realtime path: `const excluded = object.userData.worldLook === 'sky' || entity?.type === 'light'` excludes the sky box and this plugin's own marker, but not any other editor marker. Editor Markers only hides markers on `play:started`, so in EDIT MODE — where you are standing while you place and tune the light — the 12x3x12 m bomb-site boxes and ten player-sized spawn posts all get `castShadow = true`. One shadow-casting light and the viewport shows two enormous black rectangles over the bomb sites with nothing in the log to explain them.

A sun with shadows on draws no shadows at all, silently. The directional shadow frustum is derived from `range`: `far = light.range > 0 ? light.range : 60` and `half = range / 2` for the ortho box. But `range` defaults to 10 and is documented at line 104 as 'Metres to where a POINT OR SPOT light has fallen to nothing' — it has no directional meaning. A directional light placed where a sun goes, say [0, 20, 0], gets shadow camera near 0.1 / far 10 and a 10x10 m ortho box: the ground 20 m below is entirely outside the frustum, so nothing anywhere in the level is shadowed. Even with the light at head height it is a 10x10 m island of shadows on a 90 m map. Nothing is reported, which contradicts the file's own stated rule that a shadow which will not draw says so by name.

`readNumber` clamps with `Math.max(least, amount)` and says nothing when it clamps, so out-of-range numbers fail silently — the failure mode the spec names explicitly. Verified live with `{ kind:'spot', angle:-30, intensity:-5, range:-2 }`, which came back as `{angle: 0, intensity: 0, range: 0}`. Two of those are worse than merely clamped: `range: 0` is documented at line 104 as '0 never falls off', so a mistyped negative range silently becomes an UNBOUNDED light rather than a refused one; and `angle: 0` is a spot cone of zero degrees, a light that exists, costs, and illuminates nothing. Every other bad value in this file (a non-colour, a bad direction, a bad kind) is named on the console; a negative number is the one that is not.

Removing an entry from a level's `lightmaps` block cannot un-apply it. `applyLightmaps` only ever sets `entity.mesh = { ...entity.mesh, lightmap, lightmapIntensity }`; nothing ever clears a lightmap from an entity whose id has left the block. Because `mesh` is a placement key, world.js:422 `toLevel` writes that `lightmap` onto every named placement on the first save (the author acknowledges this half as p16). After that save the block is no longer 'the authority' it is described as being at line 719: delete an id from the block and the stale texture stays applied for ever, and the only way out is hand-editing up to 400 placements. Set-only application plus write-back is a one-way door.

The colour check accepts any lowercase word: `HEX.test(text) || /^[a-z]+$/i.test(text)`. Verified live — `color: 'banana'` is returned unchanged by `lights.list()`, is written into the bake manifest for the offline baker as the light's colour, and reaches `new THREE.Color('banana')`, which logs three's own 'Unknown color' and leaves the light white. The `[Lights]` colour diagnostic exists and does not fire for the case a person actually hits (a misspelled colour name); it only catches values that are not word-shaped.

`lights.report()` prints 'a hemisphere light is a global fill — its position is not read', and that is false in three. node_modules/three/build/three.module.js:22013 `WebGLLights.setupView` does `uniforms.direction.setFromMatrixPosition(light.matrixWorld)` — a HemisphereLight's world position IS its sky direction. So a hemisphere light placed below the geometry lights it from underneath with the ground colour on top, and one placed at the world origin normalizes a zero vector into a degenerate 50/50 blend. A wrong diagnostic is worse than none: it points somebody debugging 'why is my scene lit from below' away from the only line that would fix it.

`state.lightmaps` is one shared object mutated across an await, so two level loads in quick succession can interleave and apply one level's lightmaps to another level's entities. The handler resets `state.lightmaps`, awaits `context.files.read(levels/<name>.json)`, then writes `state.lightmaps.declared` and calls `applyLightmaps`. plugins/builtin/tests.js:118 loads a level per test and `runAll` reloads the original at the end, which is exactly this pattern. Latent today only because no level in the repo ships a `lightmaps` block.

`markShadowSurfaces` marks each mesh once via `object.userData.lightsShadow` and never un-marks, and the call site (line 543) is gated on `if (shadows)`. Destroying the last shadow-casting light — a flash with `shadow` opted in, or a level edit — leaves every mesh in the scene `castShadow`/`receiveShadow` true for the rest of the session, and nothing can put them back without a reload.

`const num = (value, fallback = 1) => ...` makes `boxOf` invent a 1x1x1 metre surface, silently, for any entity that has a mesh but declares no `box`, no `quad` and no collider — project/types/bomb.js:12 (`mesh: { model, tint }`) is exactly that shape. A wrong size in a manifest whose whole purpose is to be exact is worth a named line rather than a default.

BLOOD POOL IS ALWAYS UNDERGROUND. The entity:killed handler places the pool at `victim.y - 0.9`, a hardcoded half-standing-height. But damage.js calls layDown(entity, self) BEFORE it emits entity:killed (damage.js:359-361), and layDown sets `entity.y = floor + CORPSE_HEIGHT/2` with CORPSE_HEIGHT = 0.35. Verified empirically in de_dust2: victim at y=0.9, floor at y=0.0; after death victim.y = 0.175 and the decal lands at y = -0.724 — 72 cm below the floor. The pool under a body is the most-looked-at decal in a shooter and it is never visible, in any round, ever.

THREE OF THE REQUIRED GAME EFFECTS NEVER HAPPEN. `grenade:detonated` (line 696) and `bomb:exploded` (line 705) are not emitted by anything in the repo — I grepped every bus.emit in project/plugins, project/behaviours and project/types. weapons.js emits `weapon:thrown` (line 924), damage.js emits `entity:blinded` (line 544), and the bomb goes off by setting `entity.exploded = true` in project/types/bomb.js:52 with no event at all. So the spec's "a smoke grenade that actually blocks sight", "a flashbang flare" and "the bomb explosion" produce nothing in play. Consequently context.particles.blocked() — the API the brief says the bot and weapon lanes must be able to call — can never return true in a real game, because no smoke cloud is ever created. Two signals that DO exist on this bus (`entity:blinded`, `weapon:thrown`) were available and were not used.

The wall/body-hit blood decal is placed at `point.y - 1.2` with no floor query, so its height is whatever the hitbox height happened to be minus a constant. Verified: a head shot on a standing player (point.y = 1.6, floor at 0) puts the splatter at y = 0.401 — a 0.5 m horizontal quad floating 40 cm in mid-air, drawn DoubleSide with depthWrite off so it is plainly visible edge-on. A chest hit lands near 0 by luck; a leg hit (point.y ≈ 0.4) puts it at -0.8, buried. context.raycast is available and is what layDown itself uses to find the floor.

MUZZLE FLASH FILLS THE SCREEN. `at = origin + direction * 0.3` with the 'muzzle-flash' recipe at line 486 being `size: 0.4, blend: 'add'`. origin is eyeOf() = feet + 1.62 (weapons.js:94). The main camera is PerspectiveCamera(90, 1, 0.05, 400) (engine/render.js:713) at feet + eyeHeight, and de_dust2 declares eyeHeight 1.346. So the quad sits 0.406 m from the eye, 42.4 deg above the crosshair, with an angular radius of 26 deg — a bright additive #ffd9a0 slab spanning roughly 16 to 68 deg above centre, clipped by the top of a 45 deg half-FOV. It re-fires every 0.1 s on an AK and lives 3 frames of every 6. Even placed dead centre (if the eye heights are ever reconciled) 0.4 m at 0.3 m is 67% of the screen height. CS 1.6's flash is a small sprite at the gun muzzle, roughly a tenth of this.

SMOKE IS A FILL-RATE BOMB, not a draw-call one. `count: 900` with `size: [0.5, 1.1]` and `grow: 0.22` over `life: [14, 18]` means 900 camera-facing quads that reach 4.5-5.1 m across, transparent, DoubleSide, depthWrite off, packed inside a 1.1 m ball. The header solves draw calls and then ignores overdraw, which is the thing that actually kills a browser particle system: at 3 m away and t=2 s each quad already covers ~4% of the viewport, so 900 of them is ~36x full-screen overdraw, and it gets far worse as they grow and as you walk into the cloud. Real engines draw a smoke with tens of large sprites, not 900. MAX_PARTICLES 3000 allows two of these at once.

THE INVISIBLE-SMOKE BUG THE HEADER PROMISES CANNOT HAPPEN. The blocking sphere grows at `max(0.5, blocks)/1.5` = 2.67 m/s to a 4 m radius, while the visible cloud is governed by unrelated numbers (drag 1.4 and grow 0.22 at line 513). Measured, stepping the real field: t=1.5s blockedOutTo=4.00m but visibleRadius=1.68m; t=2s 4.00m vs 1.80m; t=5s 4.00m vs 2.19m; t=12s 4.00m vs 2.96m. For the whole life of the smoke there is a 1.2-2.3 m band where a player is hidden while standing outside any smoke that is on screen — exactly what the doc comment at line 290-303 says the design exists to prevent.

The cloud blocks at full 4 m radius for `now + longest` = 18 s, but the particles die between 14 s and 18 s. Measured: at t=16.0s only 463 of 900 particles remain, at t=17.9s only 25 remain (visually nothing), and blocked() still reports the full 4 m sphere throughout. For roughly the last 3 seconds of every smoke, players are invisible inside a cloud that has evaporated off the screen. Same root cause as the previous item: the blocking volume and the visible cloud are driven by two independent sets of numbers.

Cosmetic effects draw from the SHARED gameplay random stream. Measured by wrapping context.random: one bullet consumes 84 draws (6 on weapon:fired, 78 on weapon:hit), and one smoke grenade consumes 5400. That stream is the same one weapons.js:737 scatter() and applyRecoil() and the bot lane read from. Changing `wall-hit` from 10 particles to 12 — a purely visual tune — shifts every subsequent bullet's scatter and every bot decision for the rest of the round, and any future "reduce particles" quality setting would desynchronise replays outright. The engine's whole determinism doctrine (engine/loop.js header) exists to keep this kind of coupling out.

The death blood spray is emitted at `victim.y + 0.2`, which after layDown has already run is floor + 0.375 — ankle height. Combined with the underground pool, a kill produces a small spurt near the corpse's feet and nothing else. Verified: burst recorded at [-20, 0.375, 1] for a victim whose floor is y=0.

CAP = 300 is justified as "Half-Life's own r_decals default". GoldSrc's r_decals defaults to 4096, not 300 — 300 is not a Counter-Strike number and the comment invents a provenance for it. The gameplay consequence is real: 300 slots are shared by bullet holes, two blood splatters per kill and the bomb scorch, while an AK magazine alone is 30 rounds and a 5v5 round easily passes 300 shots. Holes will visibly vanish off a wall you are still shooting at, mid-firefight — the exact artefact the comment claims 300 avoids. project/tests/effects.js:35 asserts the 300, so it is now pinned.

`if (fading) revision++` fires on every fixed step for as long as ANY decal has a life, not only while one is inside its FADE_TAIL. Blood decals live 25 s (particles.js:651) and 40 s (particles.js:692), so in a match where somebody dies every few seconds the revision counter never stops moving and the painter rebuilds and re-uploads the entire decal buffer 60 times a second forever — up to 300 quads x 4 vertices x 12 floats plus four attribute uploads per frame. This directly contradicts the file's own claim that it is "rebuilt only when a revision counter moves".

The tracer is 14 static dots spread evenly along the whole shot, `speed: 0`, 3 cm each, on every single bullet. At weapons.js's shot ranges that is dots metres apart — it reads as a dotted line rather than a streak, and it does not travel. Two CS 1.6 mismatches on top of that: tracers there are drawn on a frequency (roughly every 2nd-3rd bullet, and not at all for some weapons), not on every shot; and a shotgun emits one weapon:hit per pellet (weapons.js:905-908), so an M3 blast fires 9 separate tracers plus 9 wall-hit bursts and 9 decals from one trigger pull.

Brass ejection direction is `{ x: right.x + 0.2, y: 0.7, z: right.z + 0.2 }` — a constant world-space bias added to both X and Z regardless of which way the shooter faces, so cases fly out at a different relative angle depending on your compass heading. The bias should be along `direction`/`up`, not along world axes. Also, the spawn point (line 615) is origin + right*0.15 with zero forward offset, i.e. exactly 90 deg off the view axis and therefore outside the camera frustum — the shooter never sees their own brass, which in CS you always do.

Particle gravities disagree with the world's. physics-3d defaults to -20.32 m/s^2 (the sv_gravity 800 conversion, and the value it prints in its own warning), and brass (line 495) and sparks (line 503) correctly use -20.32 — but wall-hit uses -9 and blood uses -14. Dust and blood will fall at roughly half the rate of everything else on screen, which reads as slow motion next to the brass ejected from the same shot.
The comment claims "eighteen seconds, which is how long a Counter-Strike smoke stands". 18 s is the CS:GO figure; CS 1.6's smoke is commonly cited at about 15 s. The reference for this clone is 1.6.

Silent coercion of bad option values. `grow`, `gravity`, `drag` (lines 128-130) and `spread` (line 124) all use `Number(x) || 0` with no report(), so `gravity: 'down'` or `spread: 'wide'` becomes 0 and nothing is said. physics-3d does the opposite for exactly this case ('faller has a gravity of "down", which is not a number — using -20.32 instead'), and the report() helper is already in this file and used for `at`, `colour` and unknown effect names.

asVector accepts any object, so `decals.place({ at: {} })` or a mistyped key silently places a decal at the world origin instead of being refused. The identical helper in particles.js:917 correctly requires at least one numeric x/y/z before accepting, and physics-3d refuses outright with a message explaining why moving to the origin is worse than refusing. The two files disagree with each other in the same commit.

The grade tint is applied as a straight multiply (`graded *= tint`) on a linear-light buffer, and `new THREE.Color('#ffe8c0')` with ColorManagement enabled (verified: default true in three 0.169) yields linear (1.000, 0.807, 0.527). That is a 19% cut in green and a 47% cut in blue on every pixel. A neutral linear 0.5 grey comes out at sRGB #BBAA8D. The file's own comment at line 74 calls this 'a warm cast of about two percent' and the agent's summary calls it 'a 2% warm grade'; it is off by more than an order of magnitude. Both `clean` (line 82) and `cinematic` (line 90) ship it, so the preset that is supposed to be the almost-nothing Counter-Strike look will render de_dust2 as a sepia photograph. Verified with `node -e` against the installed three.

The `Object.defineProperty(pass, 'camera', { get: () => renderer.camera })` does not do what its 6-line comment claims. SSAOPass caches `cameraNear`, `cameraFar`, `cameraProjectionMatrix` and `cameraInverseProjectionMatrix` into shader uniforms in its CONSTRUCTOR (node_modules/three/examples/jsm/postprocessing/SSAOPass.js:99-103, 131-132) and refreshes them only in `setSize()` (line 317-318) — never in `render()`. The only live read of `this.camera` is the normal-buffer render. The chain is built from `level:loaded`, and `loadLevel` forces `view.mode = 'ortho'` (engine/start-world.js:214) before emitting it, so the pass is always constructed against the OrthographicCamera (near -1000, far 1000, ortho projection). Those values persist through play mode, so SSAO reconstructs view-space positions from an orthographic inverse projection while a 90-degree perspective camera is drawing. It self-corrects only on a window resize.

`pass.uniforms.darkness.value = number(options.amount, 0.25) * 4` pushes darkness past the shader's usable range. VignetteShader computes `mix(texel.rgb, vec3(1.0 - darkness), dot(uv,uv))`, so any amount above 0.25 makes the mix target negative. `retro`'s 0.45 gives darkness 1.8, target vec3(-0.8): at the mid-edge (dot = 0.25) the result is 0.75*texel - 0.2, and at the corner (dot = 0.5) it is 0.5*texel - 0.4. The pass also runs before OutputPass, i.e. in linear light where a sand wall is ~0.2, so the entire outer half of the frame clamps to solid black. `cinematic`'s 0.3 crushes too. The x4 mapping is the defect; amount is not controllable above 0.25.

The ambient-occlusion map is loaded through `extraTexture(..., surface.map, { linear: true })`, which copies the albedo's repeat (line 570) and leaves `texture.channel` at three's default of 0. Verified by construction: the built MeshStandardMaterial has `aoMap.channel === 0` and `aoMap.repeat === [3,2]`. Channel 0 is the metre-scale tiling UV set, so an occlusion bake — which the plugin's own comment at line 541 calls 'an occlusion bake' — is tiled once per metre alongside the albedo instead of being read from the unique unwrap on uv1. engine/render.js:945 does exactly the opposite for lightmaps (`baked.channel = 1`) with a comment explaining that this is the failure it is avoiding. `ambientOcclusion` is a spec-required parameter and it is broken as shipped.

The header block (lines 18-24) and the agent's handover note both state that render.js 'keys its shared-material cache on the name, the texture, the tint and the tiling' and that two toons with different step counts share one material. That is false against the render.js in the tree: `materialLook` (engine/render.js:828-840) already folds EVERY non-shape key into the key, and `materialNameFor` (line 800-807) already resolves the object form to its name. The real remaining bug is different and is not described: `material` is in SHAPE_KEYS (engine/render.js:810), so keys nested inside `material: { name: 'toon', steps: 3 }` are skipped by the key loop, meaning only the OBJECT form — which this file documents as first-class at line 11 and the test asserts at line 109 — collapses different parameter values onto one shared material. The comment sends the next agent to widen a key that has already been widened, and misidentifies which syntax is broken.

`material.addEventListener('dispose', () => animated.delete(material))` and the header claim that 'the set cannot grow for the life of the page' do not hold for the materials this plugin actually produces. Mesh materials are shared and render.js never disposes them: `discard()` returns early for anything without `privateMaterial` (engine/render.js:1050), and `invalidateEverything()` (engine/render.js:882-885) clears `sharedMaterials` without disposing its contents. `invalidateEverything` runs on every `renderer.materials.register` call — nine times at handOver — and on every failed texture load. Each invalidation after the first sync orphans the previous water/pulse material into `animated`, where the frame system keeps calling `advance(time)` on a material nobody draws, forever.

`notes()` prints 'ssao before smaa is the right order' whenever both effects are present, but the plugin's own `cinematic` preset (lines 86-87) puts `smaa` first and `ssao` second. The note fires unconditionally on presence, not on order, so running `post.chain cinematic` prints a statement that the chain it just built violates.

`passes.set(built)` replaces the chain without disposing the passes it is replacing. `apply()` disposes only the STALE build (line 337, the losing side of a race); a superseded chain is dropped on the floor. render.js only calls `composer.dispose()` when the new list is empty (engine/render.js:1585-1591) and otherwise builds a fresh EffectComposer over the old one. So every `post.chain <preset>` — the round-trip tuning loop the header advertises at lines 30-35 — leaks a composer, two half-float render targets, and each pass's own targets (SSAO alone holds three).

The unknown-name fallback assertions (lines 63-75) exercise `materials.resolve`, which is only reachable through `context.materials.build`. Grepping the whole repo, nothing outside this test calls `context.materials.build` or `.resolve` — render.js does its own lookup with `materialNameFor` and emits its own '[render] ... no material named' report at engine/render.js:916-918. So the spec bullet these checks are written for is satisfied by render.js, not by this plugin, and the '[Materials]' prefix the test asserts at line 69 is a message a running game will never see. The assertions are real, but they read as coverage of the shipping path and are not.

`waterFlow`'s documented unit is wrong. The returned u/v are written straight to `Texture.offset` (line 746), where 1.0 is one full texture REPEAT, not one metre. On the file's own water example (`quad: [4, 4]`, line 10) render.js resolves a quad's default tiling to 1/w = 0.25 repeats per metre (engine/render.js:570), so `speed: 0.06` scrolls at 0.24 m/s — four times the documented rate, and the rate changes with the quad's size. The docstring at line 131 says 'metres of scroll per second' and project/tests/materials.js:135 asserts that message, so the test signs off on a unit claim that only holds when tiling happens to resolve to 1.

`smoothstep(1.0 - outlineWidth, 1.0, rim)` where `rim = 1 - abs(NdotV)`. With the documented `outline: 0.4` (line 9) the ramp starts at rim 0.6, i.e. every fragment whose normal is more than ~53 degrees off the view direction. On a level built from boxes, that is most of every wall in a corridor, so the effect paints wide dark bands across whole faces rather than a silhouette. The comment at lines 616-618 only discusses the head-on case, where it correctly draws nothing; the oblique case is the one you actually get and it is not mentioned.

The outline is injected at `#include <dithering_fragment>`, which in three's toon fragment shader comes after `<opaque_fragment>`, `<tonemapping_fragment>`, `<colorspace_fragment>`, `<fog_fragment>` and `<premultiplied_alpha_fragment>` (verified in node_modules/three/src/renderers/shaders/ShaderLib/meshtoon.glsl.js:111-116). So when drawing straight to the canvas `gl_FragColor.rgb` is already sRGB-encoded, while `outlineColour` is a THREE.Color in linear working space. The default #000000 is unaffected, but any non-black `outlineColour` mixes two different colour spaces and comes out too dark. It also lands after fog, so the outline is not fogged.

A zero-valued bare option still builds the full pass. `{ "bloom": 0 }` sets strength 0 and then constructs an UnrealBloomPass (five mip-level blur passes and their render targets) that costs full price to add nothing; `{ "vignette": 0 }` likewise adds a full-screen ShaderPass. Given that the header's central promise (lines 42-53) is that an unused effect costs nothing, writing 0 to turn something off — the obvious reading of a bare-number syntax — is the one way to pay for it anyway. `false` is handled at line 255; `0` is not.

MISSING CS 1.6 BUNNY-HOP CAP. PM_Jump in CS 1.6 begins with PM_PreventMegaBunnyJumping(): if |velocity| > 1.7 * maxspeed (425 u/s = 10.8 m/s) the whole velocity is scaled to 0.65 * that. It is the single thing that stops bunny-hopping from being a speed cheat, and it is absent here. Verified by driving the behaviour directly (feet-on-floor integrator, 1/60 s, gravity -20.32): with a perfect air-strafe (wish direction held perpendicular to velocity, which is the mathematically optimal case and what a good bhopper approximates) speed grows without bound as sqrt(hops) — 8.0 m/s after 1 hop, 12.5 after 5, 16.5 after 10, 22.4 after 20, 31.1 m/s (1223 u/s, 4.9x running speed) after 40. Even a crude fixed-turn-rate strafe (0.09 rad/step, the test's own technique) settles at 11.9 m/s = 1.87x, past CS's 1.7x ceiling and held there indefinitely. In CS the crop fires on every jump above the threshold so chained hops settle at ~1.1x maxspeed. A player who can bhop crosses de_dust2 at five times running speed, arrives before the round timer expects, and is untrackable — this is not a tuning difference, it is a different game.

DUCK-JUMPING GAINS NO HEIGHT. resize() shifts entity.y by (newHeight - oldHeight)/2 unconditionally, so the feet always stay put and only the head moves. That is correct on the ground and wrong in the air. HL/CS PM_Duck applies the origin shift only inside `if (pmove->onground != -1)`; in mid-air the origin is left alone and the hull shrinks about the centre, lifting the feet 18 units (0.457 m). That lift IS the duck-jump, and it is how a CS player gets on top of things. Measured through the behaviour: apex of the feet is 1.085 m with a plain jump and 1.085 m with a duck held through the jump — identical. physics-3d cannot make up the difference either: stepUp() is passed mayStep = 0 unless the body was grounded at the start of the step (physics-3d.js:320), so there is no step-up in mid-air. de_dust2 as built contains 5 colliders whose tops sit at 1.30 m, plus one each at 1.33, 1.53, 1.60, 1.67 and 1.77 m — every one of them is inside CS's duck-jump reach (1.14 + 0.457 = 1.60 m) and above this engine's 1.085 m plain-jump reach. Those boxes cannot be climbed.

WEAPON RECOIL STEERS THE PLAYER'S MOVEMENT. entity.aimYaw is taken from context.camera.aim(), and camera.js:152 defines aim() as `view.yaw - appliedYaw + punchYaw` — i.e. the player's aim WITH the recoil punch folded in. counter-strike-movement.js:145-150 builds the entire wish basis from that yaw, so the direction the body walks swings with the spray. weapons.js:707 punches the camera to the absolute pattern yaw and the AK/Galil pattern sways to +/-6 degrees (weapons.js:143-158, `sway: 6`), so at 6.35 m/s the movement direction is deflected by up to 6 degrees — about 0.66 m/s of lateral drift — and a counter-strafe fired mid-spray is aimed 6 degrees off the velocity it is meant to cancel, leaving residual sideways speed at the exact moment accuracy matters. Real CS does not do this: punchangle is applied to the view and to the shot, but PM_Move runs on v_angle without it. The file's own comment at line 111-112 asserts the opposite of what the code does ("Steering off view.yaw would let a muzzle climb walk the player sideways") — aim() is the one of the two that contains the punch. Confirmed live: de_dust2's camera follows "you", the counter-terrorist that carries player-controlled, so camera.target === entity and the punch is applied. It also feeds entity.rotation (line 119), so the third-person body model and the radar facing tick twitch +/-6 degrees during every spray, and it is an asymmetry between human and bot — bot-brain writes a clean aimYaw.

attack2 IS DEAD IN THE WHOLE GAME. The spec assigned secondary fire to this lane. The code calls context.weapons.secondary(entity), but the weapons surface published at weapons.js:1092-1107 is { table, get, give, fire, reload, select, drop, prepare, damageTo, falloff, hitboxAt, slots, sprayResetSeconds } — there is no `secondary`, and grepping project/plugins and project/behaviours finds nothing anywhere that reads the attack2 action or acts on it. So the AWP and Scout scope, the USP silencer, the Glock burst and the Famas burst are unreachable by any input, even though eleven weapons carry `zoom: true` (weapons.js:387, 396, 409, 420, 428, 439). The behaviour reports the gap once by name, which is the right failure mode, but the deliverable is not wired.

DUCKING IS INSTANT. duck() swaps the hull the same step wishCrouch goes true. HL/CS gates it on TIME_TO_DUCK = 0.4 s while on the ground (PM_Duck runs a flDuckTime countdown and only then sets usehull = 1); it is instant only when airborne. Free instant crouching makes crouch-spam and duck-peeking strictly stronger than in Counter-Strike, where the 0.4 s is what makes committing to a duck a real decision. The speed penalty is applied on the same instant step too, so tapping crouch is a free brake with no commitment.

Edges are derived from input.held() sampled once a fixed step, so any press-and-release shorter than 16.7 ms is dropped entirely — no shot, no jump, no slot change. buy-menu.js:679-689 already solves the exact problem the header comment describes (pressed() firing repeatedly across the several fixed steps in one frame) with a `spent` Set cleared on step:end, which catches sub-step taps as well. The chosen approach trades one failure for another rather than removing it. Low practical impact today because no wheel action is bound to jump, but it is a real dropped-input path.

One fixed step (16.7 ms) of input latency in the shipping level. de_dust2.json:6643 attaches player-controlled from the placement; world.js:206-207 ranks placement-added behaviours after type-declared ones, so counter-strike-movement (terrorist.js:47) runs before the keyboard is read and every key lands one step late. The header documents it honestly and the constraint is real, but it is unfixed and it is exactly the class of thing a Counter-Strike player feels without being able to name. A `player-terrorist` / `player-counter-terrorist` type declaring the two behaviours in the right order would remove it.

entity.moveSpeed is the horizontal speed whether or not the body is on the ground, so the sound lane it is declared for (line 34-35) will play footsteps through the whole of a jump. Nothing consumes it today — counter-strike-hud.js:1214 deliberately computes its own groundSpeed from the integrated velocity instead — so the field currently has no reader at all, and the one contract it exists to serve is the one it will get wrong.

aimPitch is never written. bot-brain.js:152 writes entity.aimPitch beside entity.aimYaw and weapons.js:679 reads `(entity.aimPitch ?? 0)` on the non-camera path, so a human whose camera is not currently following them (spectate, death cam, or any future body swap) shoots along pitch 0 while a bot in the same situation shoots correctly. The pair aimYaw/aimPitch is one fact; writing half of it is the same class of split the file's own header warns about.

groundAcceleration 5.5 — CS 1.6's sv_accelerate default is 5 (Half-Life's is 10; CS lowered it). The value came from the brief and was kept, and the effect is small (top speed in ~11 steps instead of ~12), but it is a movement constant that is off against the reference and the agent's report claims every number except the jump is faithful. sv_stopspeed 2.54 m/s (100 units) is likewise Half-Life's default rather than CS 1.6's 75; also inherited from the brief.

The `alreadySaid` dedupe set is module-level, not per-world, and is never cleared. The same pattern is in terrorist.js:25 and counter-terrorist.js:19 (`saidNoWeapons`). After a hot reload or a level change within one session a genuinely missing context.weapons / context.input / context.camera is reported zero times, so the second failure of the session is silent. Behaviour bags or a bus listener on level load would keep the message honest.

VERIFIED, and it is the exact failure the file's own comments claim to prevent: B,4,3 buys the AK-47 and leaves the player holding a KNIFE. press() closes the menu in the same fixed step the purchase lands. Fixed systems run BEFORE entity update hooks (engine/start-world.js:108-114), so by the time behaviours/player-controlled.js:160 checks `context.buyMenu?.isOpen === true` it is already false, falls through to the slot loop, and `tapped('slot3')` fires because Digit3 went down this step. weapons.js:499 has SLOTS[2]='knife'. Driven live on de_dust2: after tapping KeyB, Digit4, Digit3 -> primary='ak47', money 5000->2500, current='knife'. Same leak for any purchase on digit 3, 4 or 5 (knife, grenade, bomb). The menu must keep the digits for the rest of the step (defer close, or publish 'the numbers were mine this step').

The defusal kit is $200 for nothing. ITEMS['defusal-kit'] declares field:'defusalKit' and deliver() (line 462) writes entity.properties.defusalKit, but project/plugins/match-rules.js:619 reads `entity.hasDefuseKit` to choose DEFUSE_KIT_SECONDS(5) over DEFUSE_SECONDS(10) — and match-rules.js:31 names the buy menu as the writer: 'entity.hasDefuseKit halves the defuse — the buy menu sets this'. Nothing in project/ reads `defusalKit`. A CT buys the kit, is charged, and still defuses in 10 seconds. Silent: no error, no refusal, and the purchase reports ok:true.

The buy-time rule contradicts the lane that owns rounds, despite the summary claiming 'the rule and the scoreboard cannot disagree'. match-rules.js:57 sets BUY_SECONDS=15 from round start and publishes the countdown as world.state.buyTime (match-rules.js:753). buy-menu ignores buyTime/buyEndsAt entirely and invents BUY_SECONDS_AFTER_ROUND_START=90 measured from freeze ending. Verified live: 15 s into a live round, world.state.buyTime is 0 and menu.isBuyTime() is true and the AK-47 is SOLD. It also allows 90 s AFTER freeze rather than 90 s from round start, so even taken alone it is ~96 s, not 1.6's mp_buytime. The reads it does perform (world.state.phase) are the right idea aimed at the wrong field.

`liveSince` is initialised the first time isBuyTime() is asked, not when the round goes live, and nothing polls it — readKeys only reaches it on a B press, view() never calls it, and the frame system only draws. So the 90-second window starts from whenever somebody first tries to buy: press B for the first time deep into a live round and you get a fresh 90 seconds. `lastPhase` and `liveSince` are also never reset on 'level:loaded' while the loop clock restarts at 0 (engine/loop.js reset), so after a reload `context.time - liveSince` is negative and the live-round check passes for the whole next match. Found by reading; the end-to-end repro is masked because match-rules ends the round first, but the state is wrong either way.

Ammunition economy is wrong twice over. (a) Flat $60 primary / $40 secondary regardless of calibre; 1.6 prices ammo per calibre — 9mm $20, .45 $25, .357 $30, .50AE $40, 5.7mm $50, 5.56mm $60, 12ga $65, 7.62mm $80, .338 (AWP) $125 — and weapons.js declares no `ammoPrice`, so the fallback is always what runs. (b) deliver()'s ammunition branch (lines 435-449) refills the ENTIRE reserve for one payment instead of selling one magazine. Verified live: with the AK reserve emptied, one $60 purchase restored it to 90 rounds; in 1.6 that is three clips of 7.62mm at $80 = $240. An AWP reload is $60 here against $125/clip. Buying ammo is roughly a quarter of its real cost, which is exactly the kind of number that quietly rewrites the force-buy round.

Digits that land inside one frame are consumed in ascending numeric order (WATCHED is built from MENU_KEYS at line 88: 1,2,...,9,0) rather than in the order they were pressed — `pressed()` is a Set membership test with no ordering, and readKeys walks its own list. Verified live: with the menu open and Digit4 and Digit3 pressed inside one frame, the menu opened Sub-machine guns on the 3 and bought the 4th entry on the 4 — a P90 for $2350 instead of an AK-47. Needs both keys inside one frame, so it takes a stutter, a dropped frame or the backgrounded-tab timer path; but B,4,3 turning into a P90 is precisely the muscle-memory failure this plugin exists to protect.

Night vision is $1250 for nothing. It writes entity.properties.nightVision (line 462) and no file under project/ ever reads nightVision — no renderer path, no HUD, no post-processing hook. Unlike the defusal kit no other lane has claimed the field, so this is a dead purchase rather than a broken contract, but it still charges the player and reports ok:true.

Buying armour you already have is charged in full. The armour branch assigns damageable.armour = 100 unconditionally, with no check on current armour, so a player at 100 armour can be sold kevlar again for $650 (and kevlar+helmet for $1000 with a helmet already on). 1.6 refuses the sale in that state. 100 armour is the correct 1.6 value and the field names match behaviours/damageable.js — only the already-have check is missing.

The central claim of the spec — 'a bot buys through exactly the same path a human does' — is not true of the shipped game. bot-brain's buy() calls context.weapons.give(entity, wanted) directly, so bots receive a free AK-47/M4A1 every round with no money spent, no team check, no buy zone and no buy time, while a human pays $2500 through context.buyMenu.buy. Nothing in project/ except behaviours/player-controlled.js:160 (which only reads isOpen) touches context.buyMenu. The door is correctly built and has no real caller. The fix belongs to the bot lane, but the buy-menu summary should not be read as if this were done.

The test asserts menu.primaryOf(human) === 'ak47' but never asserts what the player is HOLDING (entity.carriesWeapons.current). That is the single gap that let the knife defect through 51 green assertions: the slot is right, the hands are wrong. The same omission covers the bot path at line 190. One `test.is(human.carriesWeapons.current, 'ak47', ...)` after the B,4,3 sequence would have failed loudly.

The defuse kit does nothing. This reads `entity.hasDefuseKit`, but the only thing in the project that sells a kit is buy-menu.js:133 `{ 'defusal-kit': ... field: 'defusalKit' }`, and buy-menu.js:462 writes it as `entity.properties.defusalKit = true`. `grep -rn 'hasDefuseKit' project/` returns three hits, all inside match-rules.js — nothing anywhere writes the field. So a CT pays $200 and still defuses in 10 s, silently. The spec singles this out ('5 s with a defuse kit — which is why the kit is worth buying') and it is the one branch of the plant/defuse code the test never exercises, so nothing catches it.

Nothing restores the round-start loadout, so death is nearly free and the economy the rest of this file implements has no teeth. `beginRound` revives and re-places every combatant but never touches the inventory, and `carries-weapons.js:80` hands out knife+pistol only in `start`, which runs once per level load. damage.js `die()` calls `weapons.drop(entity)`, and weapons.js:1066 drops only `bag.current` and refuses to drop a knife. Net: (a) die holding a rifle and you keep your pistol, so the loss bonus ladder, saving and force-buying are all decorative; (b) die holding your pistol (i.e. every eco round) and `bag.secondary` is nulled with nothing to refill it — you are knife-only for the rest of the match, permanently, with no error anywhere. In 1.6 you drop everything and respawn with the team pistol and knife every round.

Spawn facing is silently discarded from round two onward. `placeAtSpawn` writes `entity.rotation = spawn.rotation ?? entity.rotation`, but `rotation` is a derived field in this project, not the authority: counter-strike-movement.js:200 reads `entity.aimYaw` first and only falls back to `rotation`, and both player-controlled.js:115-119 and bot-brain.js:151-153 overwrite `entity.rotation` from their own `aimYaw` every single step. bot-brain seeds `self.aimYaw` from `entity.rotation` once, in `wake()` (bot-brain.js:158, guarded by `if (self.aimYaw === undefined)`), so it never re-reads it. de_dust2 gives every spawn-point a deliberate yaw (200/210/225/235/250 for T, 20-70 for CT); all of it is honoured on round 1 and thrown away on rounds 2-30. Every player and bot respawns facing wherever they were looking when they died.

Freeze time stops movement and nothing else, so you can shoot people during it. `holdStill` pins the body and sets `entity.frozen`, but `grep -rn '\.frozen' project/` shows match-rules.js is the only file in the project that ever reads that field — player-controlled.js:146 calls `weapons.fire(entity)` with no phase or frozen check, and weapons.js has no reference to `context.match` at all. A kill landed during freeze is still paid: damage.js:373 calls `context.match.killed` unconditionally and `settleDeath` (line 461) is not phase-gated. The lane that owns the rule published a flag and shipped without the one consumer that makes it a rule; six seconds of the round are 'frozen' in position only.

The half-time swap changes `properties.team` but not the body, so from round 16 every player fights in the enemy's skin. `swapSides` flips `entity.properties.team` on a `terrorist`-typed entity, and the mesh (`terrorist.glb`, tint #9c7b4a) is a property of the type, which nothing changes. Verified by running `node bin/engine.mjs --headless run match.round 16 --level de_dust2`: `terrorist-0..4` come back with `"team":"counter-terrorist"` and `you` (a counter-terrorist entity, the human) comes back `"team":"terrorist"` holding the C4. Team logic itself is consistent — buy-menu.js:286, counter-strike-hud.js:1222 and radar.js:576 all read `properties.team` — so the only thing that lies is the model on screen, which is the one thing the player actually aims at. `entity.mesh` is a plain assignable field, so this is fixable here.

A dropped C4 is an invisible point, not a thing in the world. `dropBomb` records `state.bombDropped = {x,y,z}` and spawns nothing; `pickUpDroppedBomb` (line 504) requires a terrorist to walk within `PICKUP_REACH` 1.2 m of coordinates that are not drawn, not in `world.state` (see the `report` list at line 746), and not on the radar — radar.js:287 looks for an *entity* of type `bomb`/`c4` and otherwise falls back to the planted site, so it shows nothing for a dropped bomb. Recovering the bomb after the carrier dies is a core T decision in 1.6 and here it is a guessing game. The same function also does the pickup test on x/z only, so a T one floor above or below the bomb picks it up through the floor.

Buy time is published but never enforced, and the lane that does enforce it disagrees by 81 seconds. `BUY_SECONDS = 15` feeds `state.buyEndsAt` and `world.state.buyTime` (line 752), and `grep -rn 'buyTime' project/` shows nothing reads either one. The actual gate is buy-menu.js:342 `isBuyTime()`, which returns true for the whole of warmup and freeze and then for `BUY_SECONDS_AFTER_ROUND_START = 90` seconds of live play (buy-menu.js:59) — a 96-second window from round start against a spec that says 15. You can rebuy at the bomb site with a minute left on the clock, which removes the force-buy decision the spec calls out by name.

`roundEndsAt = freezeEndsAt + ROUND_SECONDS` makes the on-screen round clock read 2:01 and tick down through freeze time. counter-strike-hud.js:423-426 computes what it draws as `max(0, matchState.roundEndsAt - context.time)` with no freeze case, so at the first step of a round it renders 2:01 and reaches 1:55 only when the round actually goes live. In 1.6 the clock holds at 1:55 for the whole freeze. This file's own `world.state.roundTime` (line 751) is correct (115 during freeze) — but the HUD ignores it and writes a second, disagreeing number back into `world.state.roundSeconds` (counter-strike-hud.js:689), so `hud.read` reports two different round clocks that differ by six seconds.

'An agent must be able to reach the last ten seconds of a bomb round without playing one' is not met, and `match.plant` is a name that does not do what it says. `plant: entity => match.hold(entity)` and `defuse: entity => match.hold(entity)` are both one-step `use` stamps; neither plants nor defuses anything. There is no command that puts the bomb in the ground — `match.round` and `match.skip` cannot produce a planted state, and `bin/engine.mjs` runs exactly one op per invocation with a fresh world each time, so headless (the documented way agents work here) cannot reach a planted bomb at all. Verified: `--headless run match.skip 30 --level de_dust2` returns `bombPlantedAt: 0`.

The beep ramp is linear across the whole fuse, so it carries the wrong information. `nextBeepAt = time + fastest + (slowest - fastest) * fraction` with 1 s and 0.09 s gives 0.545 s at the halfway mark and 0.27 s with 7 s left. The 1.6 C4 holds roughly one beep a second for most of the fuse and accelerates only in the last several seconds — which is exactly why a defender across the site can tell 'time to walk' from 'time to run' by ear. Here every interval is faster than it should be from the moment of the plant, so the sound stops distinguishing the two.

`properties.fuse: 35` is inert for any bomb this game actually plants, which is the two-copies-of-one-number problem the file's own comment claims to have avoided. match-rules.js:548 writes `bomb.explodesAt = context.time + BOMB_SECONDS` immediately after spawning, so `arm()` (line 76) never fires and `fuse` survives only as the denominator of the beep fraction at line 60. Change the inspector-visible `fuse` to 45 and the bomb still explodes at 35 s while the beep ramp silently stops accelerating past ~0.79 s.

`BLAST_RADIUS = 10` metres is about 394 Half-Life units. The 1.6 C4 does `RadiusDamage` at 3.5x its 500 damage — roughly 1750 units, about 44 m — which is why the explosion in 1.6 kills defenders well outside the site rather than only those standing on the bomb. Consequence here is cosmetic rather than scoring (the round is already ended by `checkWin` line 674, and blast kills pay nobody because `teamOf(bomb)` is null), but the number is wrong against the reference.
