`match.skip` winds `freezeEndsAt`, `roundEndsAt`, `nextRoundAt` and the bomb fuse but forgets `buyEndsAt`. Verified: `--headless run match.skip 30 --level de_dust2` returns `freezeEndsAt: -24, roundEndsAt: 91` with `buyEndsAt: 15` untouched, so the reported `world.state.buyTime` claims a full buy window in a round that is thirty seconds old. The one verb whose whole purpose is arranging a round state for testing leaves an inconsistent one behind.

`match.round` applies the scores it was given and then discards them: the scores are assigned at lines 935-936 and `beginRound` at 937 calls `swapSides` for any round past 15, which swaps `scoreTerrorist` with `scoreCounterTerrorist`. Verified: `run match.round '{"round":16,"scoreTerrorist":15,"scoreCounterTerrorist":3}'` returns `scoreTerrorist: 3, scoreCounterTerrorist: 15`. Arranging the exact scoreline that matters most — match point at half time — silently produces its mirror.

The plant test proves that releasing `use` cancels, but never that moving does, so `PLANT_DRIFT` (match-rules.js:104) and the `plantAnchor` reset at line 637-640 are entirely uncovered — and the spec states the interruption rule as 'interrupted by moving'. The same file also leaves `match.state`, `match.skip` and `match.round` untested despite all three being required deliverables, and never touches the side swap or `matchEnd`, which is why the score-swap bug above survived. Two lines (`test.at` the planter 0.5 m mid-plant, then assert `plantProgress === 0`) would close the first gap.

The `revive` fallback is silent. When `context.damage.revive` is absent the function quietly does a partial revive — health and `alive` are restored, but the flattened corpse collider and the `body: 'trigger'` that damage.js:{layDown} left behind are not, because only that lane records `colliderWas`/`bodyWas`. The result is a living player who cannot block a doorway and whose hitbox is corpse-height, with nothing in `errors` to explain it. Every other absent-lane guard in this file names itself on the console; this one does not.

dim() mutates, and discard() later disposes, materials that are shared with every other copy of a GLB. dim() clones materials only on the frame userData.privateMaterial flips false->true (lines 1081-1089). For a model, that flip can happen while the holder still contains only the placeholder box — tool-transform.js:191 sets e.opacity = 0.45 on the stack-picking peek, and buildModel's GLB arrives asynchronously. Once the model lands, holder.add(instance) attaches nodes whose materials are shared with modelCache and with every other terrorist, but privateMaterial is still true, so line 1090 calls setOpacity() on those shared materials (every terrorist on the map goes translucent) and discard() line 1051 calls material.dispose() on them (every terrorist loses its material). Fix: re-run the clone when nodes are added, or set privateMaterial on the instance subtree in buildModel's onReady.

view.fov is treated as a vertical field of view; Counter-Strike 1.6's 90 is horizontal. de_dust2.json declares camera.fov: 90, camera.js:188 copies it to view.fov, and this line assigns it straight to THREE.PerspectiveCamera.fov, which three defines as the VERTICAL angle. GoldSrc default_fov 90 is horizontal at 4:3, i.e. a vertical FOV of 2*atan(tan(45)/aspect) = 73.7 deg at 4:3 and 58.7 deg at 16:9. The renderer draws 90 deg vertical, which is 121.3 deg horizontal at 16:9. There is no conversion anywhere in the file (grep for 'fov' returns this line only) and the constructor at line 713 hard-codes 90 the same way. The result is a heavily wide-angle picture: the map reads as far larger than it is, edges are distorted, and turning and strafing feel wrong. This is the 'technically correct and it will feel bad' case, and it is a one-line fix.

The fallback box for a model is drawn half underground. anchorOffset() drops the holder by half the declared height for anchor: 'feet' (line 1453 applies it, and terrorist.js/counter-terrorist.js both declare it with box [0.81, 1.83, 0.81]), but buildModel adds the placeholder Mesh at the holder's local origin. The box's centre therefore sits at the model's feet, so it spans -0.915 to +0.915 about the floor. I confirmed the GLB really is feet-origin (terrorist.glb bbox y = 0 .. 1.83), so the loaded model is placed correctly and only the box is wrong. This is the exact path the spec requires for a missing or still-loading model, and item 6 of the agent's own browser checklist would show a half-buried block. The waiting mesh needs position.y = -anchorOffset(entity) / holderScale.

eyeHeight 1.346 is not Counter-Strike's standing view height. camera.js:427 computes view.y = feet + eyeHeight, so this is measured from the floor. In GoldSrc the standing hull is 72 units with VEC_VIEW 28 above a centre origin, putting the eye at 64 units = 1.626 m. 1.346 m is 53 units — 28 cm too low, which changes what you can see over every crate and every wall on the map. The neighbouring crouchEyeHeight 0.762 is exactly 30 units and exactly right, which is what makes the standing value look like an arithmetic slip rather than a choice. Outside render.js, but it is a movement/sightline number and it is wrong.

anchorOffset reports a bad mesh.anchor with a raw console.error rather than through report(). anchorOffset is called from sync() once per entity per frame (line 1453), so one misspelt anchor prints roughly sixty lines a second forever. Every other reader in this file goes through report()/alreadySaid, and the file header explicitly names a scrolling console as the thing that makes the next real error go unread.

drawSize() (exported as renderer.bounds) ignores both mesh.scale and the anchor offset for models. sync() line 1461 scales a model by (entity.scale ?? 1) * mesh.scale and line 1453 offsets it by anchorOffset(), but drawSize multiplies only by entity.scale and returns a box centred on entity.y. tool-transform.js reads renderer.bounds at lines 53, 139, 266 and 289 to draw the selection rectangle, the snap guides and the scale handle, so a model with a declared mesh.scale gets a selection box of the wrong size and any feet-anchored model gets one at the wrong height.

texture() drops onFail when the file is already known to have failed: the cache-hit branch only pushes onFail while status is 'loading', and there is no else. It is safe today only because all three call sites happen to check statusOf() first (lines 908, 943, 963). Nothing enforces that, and a fourth caller that forgets reintroduces defect 1 exactly — the fortieth wall drawing as nothing at all. Calling onFail() immediately when status is 'failed' costs one line and removes the trap.

materialLook omits entity.type from the key whenever a texture is declared, but meshMaterial line 914 falls back to tint(entity.type) when that texture has failed to load. Two different types referencing the same missing file with the same resolved tiling and no declared tint therefore collide on one shared material and both draw in whichever type's colour was built first — the fallback whose whole purpose is to distinguish them.

The stated reason for the geometry cache is contradicted by the project's own data. The comment says 'A map of four hundred walls is a handful of distinct sizes'; de_dust2.json actually has 191 distinct mesh.box sizes across 247 mesh entities, 162 of them used exactly once. The cache is still bounded and still saves ~56 allocations, but the recorded rationale is false, and the same measurement is what the merge-rather-than-instance decision at line 1128 rests on — the agent's summary claims '41 of 281 entities share a size with seven others' where the real figure is 8 of 247. The conclusion (instancing is useless here) survives; the numbers written down do not.

bomb.js declares mesh: { model: 'counter-strike/models/c4.glb' } with no anchor, so anchorOffset returns 0 and the model is placed with its origin at the entity centre. c4.glb is authored base-origin (bbox y = -0.002 .. 0.093) while the collider is 0.22 m tall, so a planted C4 floats about 0.11 m above the floor. This is the failure anchorOffset's own comment describes, in the one other type that uses a model. Outside render.js, but it is the direct consequence of the anchor contract this file defines.

The spectator hand-off is one-way: the camera is never given back when you respawn. spectateWhenDead() calls context.camera.follow(teammate) on death, and the alive branch (517-523) only clears diedAt/spectating/killedBy — nothing re-follows hud.youId. camera.applyRule() runs only on 'play:started' and on a level load while running (camera.js:205,220), and match-rules starts a new round by teleporting bodies, not by reloading the level. VERIFIED headless: kill 'you', step past SPECTATE_AFTER, revive — camera.target is still 'counter-terrorist-0' after 2 more seconds. player-controlled keeps driving your own body from the same view, so for the rest of the match you turn an off-screen body while watching a bot's eyes. This is unrecoverable without a level reload.

The built-in HUD is switched off permanently and can never be handed back. The level:loaded handler does Object.assign(hud, freshHud()) on line 133, which sets tookOverHud = false, and THEN tests `if (context.hud && hud.tookOverHud)` on line 138 — so the restore is unreachable. The other restore, at line 283 in the !active path, is dead for the same reason: tookOverHud was already zeroed by the handler. VERIFIED headless: load de_dust2, step, load level1, step — context.hud.visible === false and stays false for the rest of the session. The header's promise ('A level with no Counter-Strike in it gets the built-in HUD it declared') is not kept.

A muzzle flash and a full recoil kick fire on every weapon switch to a weapon with fewer rounds loaded. The third clause of the `fired` test — (hud.lastMagazine !== null && magazine !== null && magazine < hud.lastMagazine) — reads a magazine that shrank as a shot. weapons.js:1042 sets bag.ammo = bag.magazines[wanted] on select, so AK-47 (30) -> USP (12) trips it. VERIFIED headless: switch to the pistol without firing and hud.muzzleFlashUntil jumps to time+0.05 and hud.kick to 0.554, with shotsFired still 0 and lastShotAt unchanged. The clause is also unnecessary: carries-weapons writes lastShotAt and shotsFired on every shot (weapons.js:881-882), so the first two clauses already cover it.

Sign error in the recoil: the muzzle kicks DOWN, not up. The silhouettes are drawn with the muzzle up-left of the origin and the grip at it (RIFLE.muzzle = [-150,-108], line 1110), and the pivot is the grip. g.rotate(-0.06 + reloadTilt - hud.kick * 0.09) makes the angle MORE negative on a shot, which in canvas coordinates rotates anticlockwise on screen and swings an up-left muzzle down-left. Working it through at full kick, with the outer + hud.kick * 6 * unit on line 1032, the muzzle moves from (-156.2, -98.8) to (-147.2, -70.9): 28 px DOWN at unit 1, 56 px at unit 2. Every shot makes the gun dive, which is the opposite of what the spec asked for ('a RECOIL KICK back and up') and the opposite of what a player reads as recoil. The sign wanted is + hud.kick * 0.09.

When the bomb is planted the panel turns red and the C4 blinks, but the number inside it is still the ROUND clock (roundEndsAt - context.time, set at line 425). match-rules does not extend roundEndsAt on a plant (match-rules.js:689 only ends the round `if (!planted && ...)`), so the red panel counts down to 0:00 and then sits at 0:00 while the bomb is still live. match.state.bombExplodesAt and world.state.bombTime are both published (match-rules.js:741,760) and neither is read anywhere in this file. The 35-second fuse is the only number that matters in the last part of a Counter-Strike round, and the HUD shows a dead one instead.

RANGE = 45 makes the radar a whole-map overview, not the 1.6 radar. With scale = (size/2)/RANGE (line 417) and size = 190*unit (line 412) that is 2.11 px per metre, covering 90 m across a map that measures 79 x 72 m. MEASURED on de_dust2 from the CT spawn: of the 217 shapes that survive the height banding, 153 draw thinner than one pixel — a default 0.4 m brush is 0.84 px wide — and a player dot at radius 3.6 px is 3.4 m across, wider than the corridors it stands in. The outline will read as a grey wash and the dots will overlap constantly. The source comment on line 59 ('About a third of de_dust2 across') is wrong by a factor of three; it is 114% of the map's long axis. 1.6's radar is readable precisely because it is a local view at a large scale.

The round clock includes freeze time and disagrees with the match lane's own published clock. readTheMatch counts down match.state.roundEndsAt, which match-rules sets to freezeEndsAt + ROUND_SECONDS (match-rules.js:346). MEASURED headless: during freeze the HUD reads '1:56' (2:01 at the very start of the round) while world.state.roundTime — published by match-rules for exactly this purpose, and deliberately pinned to ROUND_SECONDS during freeze at match-rules.js:751 — says 115. Two lanes, one clock, two answers, both on screen. 1.6 holds the timer at 1:55 through freeze time; 2:01 is not a Counter-Strike round length.

hud.read and the drawn HUD report different money once you have died. The canvas draws reading.money, which moneyOf() resolves for hud.youId (line 311, an id held for the whole level). The registered line '${money}' reads world.state.money, which match-rules publishes for context.camera.target (match-rules.js:729,758) — and after the spectator hand-off those are two different players. VERIFIED headless: canvas $4200 and hud.read '$800' at the same instant. The notes describe this as a few frames of load-time race; it is permanent after the first death.

publish() writes roundSeconds and crosshairGap (line 692) into world.state at three decimal places every fixed step. The built-in HUD's change-detection key is JSON.stringify(world.state) (hud.js:63), so it now stringifies the entire state — including world.state.match, which match-rules aliases in — and clears its canvas on EVERY frame, on every level, for a HUD it has been told not to draw. match-rules rounds to whole seconds specifically to prevent this (match-rules.js:749-751), and this file's own header argues against paying a JSON stringify per frame. Rounding these two to a whole second / whole pixel in world.state would restore it.

The radar picks whose radar it is with world.byId('you') as its second choice, and counter-strike-hud.js:1183-1187 spends a paragraph explaining why an entity id is deliberately not one of the answers ('right for de_dust2 and wrong for every map after it'). The two files also disagree on the third choice — the radar tests for the bag `entity['player-controlled']`, the HUD walks entity.behaviours by name. On a map with no camera target and no entity called 'you' the two can centre on different bodies, which puts one player's radar under another player's health.

knownFacing reads entity.yaw and the comment above it states that bot-brain writes `yaw` and mirrors it into `rotation`. Nothing in the project writes entity.yaw: bot-brain.js:151-153 writes entity.aimYaw and entity.rotation, and player-controlled.js:115-119 does the same. The branch is dead and the documented contract is wrong, which is worse than dead code because the next lane will believe it.

SIGHT_CONE = cos(75 degrees) gives a 150-degree spotting cone against the level's declared fov of 90 (de_dust2.json camera block). A team mate therefore reveals enemies up to 30 degrees outside each edge of their own screen, so the stated rule — 'enemies shown ONLY when a teammate can see them' — is not what happens. In 1.6 an enemy appearing on radar means somebody genuinely has eyes on them, and that reliability is what the radar is for.

Two of the thirty assertions assert nothing. Line 58, test.is(you.id, driven[0].id, 'and it is the one the camera is looking out of'), compares driven[0].id with itself: `you` is context.camera?.target || driven[0], and camera.applyRule() only runs when context.loop.running (camera.js:205), which it never is under test.simulate — VERIFIED, camera.target is null at that point, which is why line 66 has to follow(you) by hand immediately afterwards. Line 110, test.ok(/^\d+:\d\d$/.test(clock)), tests the test's own minutesAndSeconds helper rather than anything the HUD produced. The other 28 checks are real.

The renderer DOES offer a viewmodel layer, so the 2D silhouette is no longer the right answer and the plugin header (counter-strike-hud.js:38-49) now states the opposite of the truth. render.js:1255-1263 builds a second THREE.Scene with its own PerspectiveCamera(54, 1, 0.01, 20) and its own lights; 1543-1548 draws it as a second pass against a cleared depth buffer; and 1603-1653 exposes context.renderer.viewmodel.set({model, position, rotation, scale}) plus .offset(position, rotation) documented as 'Per-frame bob, sway and kick, added on top of whatever set declared' — in view space, metres and radians, which is exactly what advanceViewmodel already computes. MITIGATION, and it matters: this API is absent from HEAD and is an uncommitted change to engine/render.js timestamped 01:24, seven minutes AFTER counter-strike-hud.js (01:17), so the agent's claim was almost certainly true when it read the file. It is not true of the tree as it stands, and the spec's instruction was 'if it does, use it'. Nothing else calls renderer.viewmodel.* yet, so there is no double-gun today — but there will be the moment the weapon-model lane wires it up.

The flashbang's off-axis scaling — the one thing the spec singled out — is computed from the wrong entity. lookDirection() reads `entity.yaw` / `entity.pitch`, and NOTHING in project/ ever writes those fields: the agreed aim contract is `entity.aimYaw` / `entity.aimPitch` (written by bot-brain.js:151-152, read by weapons.js:678 and radar.js:355). So for every entity the code falls through to `context.camera.aim()` — the local player's view — and blinds every bot according to where the human is looking. Proven headless: with a body at yaw-0 facing a flash, setting `aimYaw = Math.PI` (back fully turned) leaves blindAmount at 0.797, identical to staring straight at it; only setting the unused `entity.yaw = Math.PI` drops it to 0.082. Turning away from a flash currently does nothing for anyone but the camera target.

`self.lastHurtBy = options.from` stores the killer ENTITY in a declared behaviour property, and engine/inspect.js:79 serialises the whole bag for the single-entity view. Once two players have shot each other, A.damageable.lastHurtBy → B → B.behaviours[].bag.lastHurtBy → A is circular, and bin/engine.mjs:166 stringifies the result with no guard. Proven headless: `engine.entity('turner')` serialises fine after one hit and throws `Converting circular structure to JSON` after the trade — i.e. `node bin/engine.mjs entity <player>` dies with an unhandled TypeError for any player who has been in a firefight, which is the normal state of the game and the main verb every other agent debugs with. The bridged path only survives because plugins/builtin/bridge.js:88 has a circular-safe serialiser; headless has none. Every consumer already accepts an id (counter-strike-hud.js:481 and match-rules.js:448 both resolve string-or-entity), so storing `options.from?.id ?? options.from` costs nothing.

FALL_SAFE_SPEED = 7 m/s is less than half Counter-Strike's. HL/CS use PLAYER_MAX_SAFE_FALL_SPEED = 580 units/s, and this engine's gravity is already in CS units (physics-3d.js:18, GRAVITY = -20.32 = 800 u/s²), so the correct threshold is 14.73 m/s — a 5.34 m free drop. FALL_FATAL_SPEED = 26 is right (1024 u/s), so the ramp starts in the wrong place and every fall costs roughly double. Measured in a headless world: 1.5 m drop -2.4 HP, 2 m -9.5, 3 m -20, 5.34 m (CS's exact free-drop limit) -39.8, 8 m -55.8 where CS charges 29. Worse, jumping off a 1.14 m box — the movement lane's own jumpSpeed of 6.81 m/s, counter-strike-movement.js:83, plus a de_dust2 crate — costs 11.1 HP where CS charges nothing, and a flat jump lands at 6.81 against a 7.0 threshold, so any jump off any lip bleeds health. This is technically to spec (the brief said 'about 7 m/s') and it will feel badly wrong: dropping down from anywhere in dust2 is a free move in 1.6 and a tax here.

There are two hitbox tables and the live game uses the other one. weapons.js:809 computes the body part with its OWN hitboxAt (weapons.js:85-90, head from 0.88 of body height = 1.61 m on a standing player) and passes it as an explicit `hitbox` at weapons.js:816, so damage.js's HITBOXES (head above 1.55 m) never runs on the path a bullet actually takes. Confirmed by calling both on the same point: a hit 1.56–1.60 m up a standing body is 'head' to this lane and 'chest' to the shooting lane — a 6 cm band, at exactly the height crosshair placement lives at, where the game deals 36 instead of 144. The test at project/tests/damage.js:78-91 asserts the 1.55 boundary that the shipped game does not use, so the test reads as coverage of a rule nothing enforces. One table has to be deleted; two lanes cannot each own the head.

Every bullet that hits a person now plays three sound files. playHurt() (damage.js:597-605) plays an impact (flesh/kevlar/helmet) AND a pain grunt, and weapons.js:826 plays its own impact for the same bullet immediately after calling context.damage. Verified headless: one call to context.damage on a chest produces `hit-flesh-2.wav` + `hurt-3.wav`, and the shooting lane adds a third from its own FLESH set. plugins/builtin/audio.js:82 has no throttle and no voice limit, so a 600 RPM AK spray fires 30 overlapping samples a second at a target, and there is no distance attenuation anywhere in the engine — a hit on the far side of dust2 is heard at full volume. In 1.6 you get one impact and a grunt, and both are positional.

context.damage.blast and context.damage.flash have no caller in the game. weapons.js:924 emits `weapon:thrown` for an HE grenade or a flashbang and leaves flight and detonation to 'whoever owns grenades'; grepping project/ finds no subscriber, and the only production caller of blast is match-rules.js:581 for the C4. So the grenade case and the flashbang — both explicitly required by the spec — are reachable only from project/tests/damage.js:207,217. The lane that owns explosions shipped the arithmetic and did not connect it to the one event that would fire it, and the symptom in play is a grenade that lands and does nothing, with no error anywhere.

A malformed `point` silently becomes a leg shot at 0.75x. `clamp(point.y - feet, …)` on a point with no numeric y yields NaN, `HITBOXES.find(part => NaN >= part.above)` is undefined, and the `?? HITBOXES[HITBOXES.length - 1]` fallback is 'legs', not the 'chest' used when the point is missing entirely (line 174). Nothing is reported. Verified: `context.damage(target, { amount: 10, point: 1.7 })` returns hitbox 'legs', as does `{ x, z }` with no y. That exact shape is the shooting lane's own signature — weapons.js:560 is `hitboxAt(target, pointY)` taking a bare number — so a caller who confuses the two hitboxAt functions loses a quarter of the damage with nothing in the log, in a file that otherwise names every bad input.

revive() reconstructs the feet from the CORPSE_HEIGHT constant (`entity.y - CORPSE_HEIGHT / 2`) rather than from the collider it is about to replace, so it is only correct if nothing touched the corpse's collider between death and revive. Something does: nothing in counter-strike-movement.js reads damageable.alive, so a dead player's crouch key still runs duck() and resize() (counter-strike-movement.js:304-333) on the body. Proven headless with a real `terrorist`: kill it (collider 0.35, y 0.675), set wishCrouch — the corpse halves to 0.175 and drops to 0.588 — then revive puts it back at y 1.328 instead of 1.415, i.e. 8.7 cm of the player inside the floor at round start. Reading `entity.collider.box[1] * (entity.scale ?? 1)` instead of the constant removes the coupling.

'The entity stops taking input' is not implemented; it is an accident of list order. Neither counter-strike-movement.js nor player-controlled.js mentions damageable or alive (grep finds zero hits), so a corpse is still fed wishMove/wishJump/wishCrouch every frame. The only reason it does not walk is that `damageable` is written last in the behaviour list of both types (terrorist.js:47, counter-terrorist.js:41) and zeroes the velocity the movement behaviour just wrote — reorder that list and the body slides. The crouch is not covered by the velocity trick at all and still resizes the corpse (see the revive defect).

A fall passes no `from`, so damage.js:297 leaves the previous shooter in lastHurtBy and the kill is misattributed. counter-strike-hud.js:481-490 builds the kill feed from `damageable.lastHurtBy` and `lastWeapon`, so a player you shot once and who later drops to their death is reported in the feed as your kill with the weapon 'world'. Either clear lastHurtBy for a fall or attribute it explicitly.

`entity:hurt` is emitted with the un-clamped health of a killing blow: line 291 writes `self.health = health - amount`, the event carries that value (e.g. -8), and die() only clamps to 0 afterwards at line 340. Any consumer that draws a health bar or a damage number from the event — the reason the event exists — has to clamp it itself.

The blast and flash constants are a third copy of numbers the weapons table already carries and none of the three agree. BLAST_RADIUS 7 / BLAST_DAMAGE 98 here, `blastRadius: 4.4` for hegrenade in weapons.js:459; FLASH_RADIUS 25 here, `blastRadius: 7` for flashbang in weapons.js:467. Counter-Strike's own are 250 units (6.35 m) for the HE and 1500 units (~38 m) for the flash. Nothing is reachable today (see the blast/flash defect), so this is cheap to settle now and expensive to settle once a grenade lane calls one of them.

BLOCKER — for the human player the bullets follow only about a third of the spray pattern, and not repeatably. applyRecoil punches the camera to an ABSOLUTE position (pattern[n] - punchPitch) but Game Camera decays punch with a 0.09 s time constant (plugins/builtin/camera.js:67), so by the time the next shot leaves 100 ms later only exp(-0.1/0.09)=33% of it is left, and the shot fires along that residue. Measured, held trigger, AK-47, camera following the shooter (pitch of the direction on 'weapon:fired', degrees): 0.00, 0.73, 1.66, 2.39, 2.88, 3.43, 3.16, 3.42, 3.47, 4.21, 4.21, 4.32, 4.20, 3.58 — against a pattern that says 0, 2.71, 5.10, 7.17, 8.92, 10.35, 11.47, 12.26, 12.74, 12.90. The bullets top out at 4.3 deg instead of 12.9, they are NOT monotonic (shot 6->7 goes 3.43 -> 3.16, shot 12->14 goes 4.32 -> 3.58) because the residue depends on the gap between fire() calls in fixed steps rather than on the shot number, and the rendered view sawtooths 8-9 degrees up and back every 100 ms. So the pattern in the table is not the pattern the player can learn, pulling down by what is on screen over-compensates by 3x, and 'the crosshair kicks but the bullets do not' — the exact failure the specification names — is what has been built for the only entity the camera follows.

Bots and players do not get the same recoil, despite the claim of 'the identical numbers, no private path'. aimOf has two branches: the camera-followed entity aims through camera.aim() (decayed punch, ~1/3 of the pattern, see the blocker above) while everything else aims through entity.aimYaw/aimPitch + bag.recoilPitch/recoilYaw, which is the pattern at FULL strength and does not decay at all between shots. Measured on the same shooter with the camera let go of: 0.00, 2.61, 4.99, 7.40, 8.79, 10.55, 11.35, 12.08, 12.88, 12.98 deg — i.e. exactly the pattern, three times the player's. A bot therefore sprays over your head after four rounds where a player would not, and worse, bag.recoilPitch persists until resetSpray, so a bot whose burst pause is shorter than the 0.3 s reset (bot-brain.js line 441 rests 0.15-0.35 s) keeps the whole 12.9 deg offset into its next burst.

give() on the weapon already in your hands silently throws away the magazine you paid for. give() writes bag.magazines[id] = weaponData.magazine and then calls select(), but select() returns false at this line when wanted === bag.current, so bag.ammo and bag.reserve are never re-read — and the next fire() or stow() writes the stale count straight back over magazines[id]. Verified: AK at 25/90 after five shots, weapons.give(shooter,'ak47') returns true, ammo is still 25, and it is still 25 after switching to the knife and back. buy-menu.js:427 treats that true as a delivery and buy-menu.js:522 then charges the full $2500 (nothing in buy() refuses a repeat primary — it only records `dropped`), so re-buying the gun you are holding costs a full price and does nothing at all.

damageTo() is advertised as the single copy of the armour arithmetic ('a second copy is how the AK stops one-shotting a helmet') but nothing calls it — grep over project/, plugins/ and engine/ finds exactly one caller, project/tests/weapons.js. The live path is context.damage in project/plugins/damage.js, which has its own MULTIPLIER table and its own armourAfter(), and the two have already drifted: damage.js:280 only applies armour or helmet when self.armour > 0, this line applies the helmet unconditionally. Verified against the running world — m4a1 head, armour 0, helmet true: the live path takes 100 and kills, damageTo says 92.4 and the victim lives. So the contract requirement the test proves at tests/weapons.js:214-216 ('the same shot from an M4 does not' kill a helmeted player) is decided in the game by a different function, and it is false there once the victim's kevlar has been shot off.

There is no secondary attack on the weapons surface. project/behaviours/player-controlled.js:149-150 calls context.weapons.secondary(entity) for attack2 and reports by name on the console that 'the silencer, the scope and the burst have no key' — the surface published here is table/get/give/fire/reload/select/drop/prepare/damageTo/falloff/hitboxAt/slots/sprayResetSeconds and nothing else. The table promises the feature anyway: zoom: true on scout, awp, aug, sg552, g3sg1 and sg550, silencedSound on usp and m4a1. Nothing implements either, so an AWP is a hipfire rifle with a 0.12 degree cone, the Scout and AUG never scope, the Glock and FAMAS have no burst, and the knife has no stab (the 65-damage back stab, which is a real CS mechanic, does not exist).

The pattern's climb is eased OUT, so 21% of the whole rise lands between shot 1 and shot 2: pitch = climb*(1-(1-n/climbShots)^2) gives the AK 2.71, 5.10, 7.17, 8.92 ... 12.90 degrees. At 20 m the second bullet is 95 cm above the first, which makes the two- and three-round burst — the standard way of using a rifle beyond 25 m in 1.6, where the first few bullets land close together and the climb steepens after them — useless. The comment's reasoning is also wrong: tapping is accurate because the bullet leaves before the kick (fire() line 889-908) and because the pattern resets, not because the curve is front-loaded.

Two hitbox tables with different boundaries. Here the head starts at 0.88 of body height (1.61 m on a 1.83 m body); project/plugins/damage.js:38 starts it at 1.55 m absolute, and that lane's own test asserts 1.56 m is a head (project/tests/damage.js:81). Gunfire names the hitbox so this file wins for bullets, but anything that passes a point instead gets the other answer, and the 6 cm band between 1.55 and 1.61 m is a chest to a rifle and a head to everything else. One of the two tables should be deleted rather than both kept.

The grenade radii are roughly half of Counter-Strike's and disagree with the damage lane's own constants, which are the ones actually in force: hegrenade blastRadius 4.4 m here against damage.js:95 BLAST_RADIUS 7 and 1.6's 350 units (8.9 m); flashbang 7 m here against damage.js:97 FLASH_RADIUS 25; c4 12 m (line 485) against 1.6's ~1000 units (25 m). Nothing consumes the table's numbers yet, so today they are inert — which is exactly how a wrong number survives to the day something starts reading it.

alreadySaid is a module-level Set that is never cleared, so every [weapons] fault is reported once per PROCESS. In an editor session that loads a second level, or a test run that walks several levels, a missing raycast, a missing context.damage or an entity with no carrying behaviour is announced for the first level and silent for every level after it. plugins/builtin/physics-3d.js:502-505 clears exactly this on 'level:loaded' and says why — 'the next level gets told about its own problems rather than inheriting a silence'.

prepare() adopts whatever object happens to be at entity.carriesWeapons, so the promise that give() refuses a non-carrier by name does not hold. buy-menu.js:394 invents a stand-in bag { grenades: [] } when the field is missing; prepare() fills it in, inventoryOf() is satisfied and the report at line 643 never fires — so the purchase succeeds on an entity with no 'carries-weapons' behaviour, and that entity then has no update hook, so its reload never completes, its spray never goes cold and its moveSpeedFactor is never written. The same hole is open the other way: carries-weapons.js:60 leaves entity.carriesWeapons pointing at an orphaned bag after the behaviour is detached.

The inaccuracy cone never grows with sustained fire — it depends only on stance and speed, so with the pattern learned the 25th bullet of a spray is exactly as accurate as the 1st. In 1.6 the cone opens as you keep the trigger down, and that is half of why long-range spraying loses to tapping. Measured on the running world with recoil zeroed, AK on a wall at 20 m (metres from the group centre, median/worst): standing 0.055/0.085, crouched 0.020/0.030, walking 3.2 m/s 0.183/0.255, running 6.35 m/s 0.316/0.447, airborne 0.508/0.672. The four states are modelled and correctly ordered, but the moving numbers are forgiving — 28% of a running AK's bullets land inside a 0.45 m torso at 20 m and 77% while walking, where 1.6 would put run-and-gun in the single digits — so peek-and-strafe-shoot will beat stop-and-shoot in a way it does not in the original.

fire() returns false with no word when bag.current names a weapon the table does not have (or is empty). Every other refusal in this file either is an ordinary game state or reports by name; this one is the case where something upstream has written a wrong id, and it presents as a trigger that does nothing for the rest of the round.

buy() arms every bot for free. It calls `context.weapons.give(entity, 'ak47'|'m4a1')`, and give() bypasses money entirely — buy-menu.js:22 says `context.buyMenu.buy(entity, id)` is "the only one that buys" and it is the only path that calls match.pay. Verified by simulating de_dust2 headless: at round 1 freeze every bot reads `{primary:'ak47'|'m4a1', money:800}` — a $2500 AK and a $3100 M4 handed out on the pistol round, and again free after every death (revive clears `primary`). The human on `player-controlled` starts the same round with $800 and a USP and must actually pay. The file's own comment two lines up claims "a bot that paid itself would be a second economy running beside the real one" — it created a free one instead, which is worse, and it makes the pistol round and every eco round meaningless.

The bomb-site flip oscillates; the comment claiming otherwise is wrong. `if (site && !carrying && near(entity, site, 8)) { self.site = self.site === 'A' ? 'B' : 'A' }` fires the moment a non-carrier gets within 8 m of a site centre — which is exactly the half-width of site A's 16x16 trigger, so the bot turns around on the site's doorstep. Arriving at the other site flips it straight back. Verified with one blind, unkillable CT alone on de_dust2: over 110 s it flipped at t=10 (7.9 m from B), walked 45 m to A, flipped at t=54 (7.6 m from A), walked back, flipped again at t=106 — three full map crossings, never once standing on a site. The comment says "the decision is recorded, so it cannot flip back the moment it walks away"; nothing records that this site has already been visited, so it flips back every lap. In a busy round combat masks it (0–4 flips per bot per 120 s) because `hunt`/`engage` outrank `advance`, but a CT that is left alone never holds a site, which is the whole CT game.

A bot that reloads in a firefight turns its back and jogs to the objective. decide() returns 'reload' at line 276/277 BEFORE the `if (self.target)` check at 279, so an empty magazine outranks a live enemy for the entire reload (2.1–4.5 s off the weapon table); the 'reload' case then calls `walkTo(entity, context, self, objective(...))` and `turnTowardsTravel(...)`, which aims at `self.travelYaw` — the direction of travel — not at the target. Verified by holding magazines at 2 rounds during a headless soak: e.g. `t=10.4 counter-terrorist-0 reloading, enemy 25.1m away, body pointed 41 deg off it, speed 5.0` — 17 bot-seconds of it in 60 s. It never happens with a full 30-round rifle, which is only because of the free-rifle defect above; with a pistol, a Deagle or an eco round it is the normal case.

`regionAt` is implemented but never contributed, so the promised function does not exist. The wrapper assigned to `context.navigation` (lines 593–602) forwards only path / walkable / nearest / regions / cellSize / stats / rebuild. Verified at runtime after loading de_dust2: `Object.keys(context.navigation)` is `path, walkable, nearest, regions, cellSize, stats, rebuild` and `typeof context.navigation.regionAt === 'undefined'`. The agent's summary states it "contributes context.navigation.path/walkable/nearest/regionAt/stats". Any other lane that takes that at face value gets a TypeError. The implementation at line 334, and its docstring telling callers to prefer it over `path`, are unreachable dead code; `emptyNavigation` (line 500) does not define it either.

"every step of the route is walkable" cannot fail — it is a tautology dressed as the spec's explicit requirement. `path()` returns `point(index)` for open cells only: `{x: centreX(index), y: floor[index], z: centreZ(index)}` (bot-navigation.js:217). `walkable(where)` then does `indexAt(at.x, at.z)`, which is `Math.floor((centreX - minX)/cellSize)` = the same index, checks `open[index]` (necessarily 1) and `withinReach(index, {y: floor[index]})`, which compares floor[index] against `floor[index] - stepHeight` and `floor[index] + playerHeight` — both trivially satisfied. There is no input for which offMap.length can be non-zero. The check that would have had teeth — that a real 0.81 m hull fits at each point, or that consecutive points are joined — is not made. (I wrote that check myself against the level: it passes today, 0 of 8900 cells, so the underlying navigation is sound; the assertion still proves nothing.)

Hearing reads the wrong field: `if (carry && carry.nextShotAt > context.time) return GUNFIRE_HEARD`. `nextShotAt` is a refire/deploy gate, not a "just fired" stamp — weapons.js:1045 sets it to `context.time + deploySeconds` (0.4–0.7 s) on every `select()`, and weapons.js:919 sets it to `time + 1` on a grenade throw. So a silent weapon switch, a bomb draw or a grenade throw reads to every enemy inside 45 m as gunfire, with the switcher's exact position. `carry.lastShotAt` is on the same bag (weapons.js:882) and is the field that means what this line wants.

Bots fire while sprinting, which the specification forbids outright. Inside STAND_STILL_RANGE (12 m) `act` calls `strafe()`, which writes `wishStrafe = ±1` and never sets `wishWalk`, so the body accelerates to the full 6.35 m/s ground speed; `shoot()` (line 419) has no speed gate at all. weapons.js coneOf() then multiplies the cone by `1 + speed/6.35 * 4` = 5x. It also reads as a machine rather than a person: a Counter-Strike player counter-strafes to a stop before shooting, and this bot jitter-strafes at a full run for the whole duel.

'cover' does not take cover. It walks to `entity + (entity - target)` — straight backwards along the enemy's sightline, in the open, with `turnTowardsTravel` not called so the body keeps facing the shooter. Nothing in the file ever asks whether a candidate position breaks line of sight, even though `context.raycast` is already in hand at line 234. Combined with 'engage' (line 314: stop dead beyond 12 m, strafe inside it) no state ever moves a bot behind geometry, so the spec's "take cover" and "how well it uses cover" scale by skill are not implemented — the bot retreats in a straight line while being shot at, which is the worst available move.

A bot that runs out of ammunition entirely never switches weapon. `shoot()` returns on `carry.ammo === 0`, and decide() only returns 'reload' when `carry.reserve > 0` (line 277), so a bot with an empty magazine and an empty reserve falls through to 'engage' and stands there tracking the enemy with a dead gun forever. `context.weapons.select(entity, slot)` is called exactly once in the file, for the bomb (line 342); the pistol and the knife are never drawn.

The fire gate and the shot use different aims. `entity.aimYaw`/`aimPitch` are written after `act()` has already run, so `context.weapons.fire(entity)` (called from shoot(), line 437) reads the PREVIOUS step's aim off the entity (weapons.js:678 aimOf) while shoot()'s acceptance test at lines 429–430 used this step's `self.aimYaw`. `player-controlled` writes aim at line 113–120 and fires at 146, i.e. in the correct order, so a human's shot uses the current aim and a bot's does not — an asymmetry the file's own preamble says must not exist. Measured over 85 bot shots in a 60 s soak the discrepancy is small (median 0.02 deg, max 0.54 deg) because the aim has converged by the time the reaction timer expires, so the impact is bounded; the ordering is still wrong.

Every failed stuck check throws the path away (`self.stuck++; self.path = null`), which forces a full A* over 8,900 walkable cells on the next step. Nothing in the brain separates bots from each other, so the shipped level's nine bots converge on one objective and jam: in a headless run I watched four CTs and three Ts pile inside 2 m of the planted bomb, all bunny-hopping, with stuck counts climbing to 5 while each re-ran A* every 0.6 s. The claimed "soak counts sit at 0-2" holds in a normal match only because bots rarely survive to reach the objective together.

The comment states a number the code does not implement: "it also keeps bots half a metre back from a drop". SUPPORT_REACH is 0.3 (line 61), so a cell centre is at least 0.30 m from the edge of the floor, not 0.5 m — and less than the 0.38 m half-width the clearance test uses on the same footprint, so the outer 0.105 m of a real 0.405 m half-hull may overhang the drop at a legal waypoint.

The clearance tolerance has the wrong sign for the failure mode the specification names. PLAYER_HALF_WIDTH is 0.38 against a real 0.81 m hull, and clearAbove() (line 472) subtracts SKIN 0.02 on top, so the effective half-width is 0.36 m: a 0.72 m gap is marked walkable for a body that needs 0.81 m. The comment justifies this as avoiding "a corridor that measures right on paper and cannot be walked", but an optimistic navmesh produces exactly that — a bot routed into a doorframe, which is the failure the brief says destroys the illusion. A pessimistic value (0.41+) loses a legal doorway instead, which is the cheaper error. I checked all 8,900 open cells against a true 0.405 m half-hull with no skin and found 0 mismatches, so it is latent on de_dust2 today and will bite on the first map with a 0.75 m gap in it.

The refusal message tells the user to "press FOCUS in the toolbar while the game is running", but that button is invisible and unclickable at exactly the moment the message is printed. The refusal only happens when play was started without a gesture — and by then shell.focus(true) has already run, so engine/style.css:116 (`.app.focused .bar > * { display:none }`) has hidden every toolbar child except `.play`; the FOCUS menu button carries class `menu`, so it is gone. Reproduce: `node bin/engine.mjs run engine.play` (or `engine.play()` in the console) -> frame collapses, browser refuses fullscreen, console says press FOCUS, FOCUS is not on screen. The only visible control is STOP, which also ends the round. The spec's one hard requirement for this path — say what the user should do — points at a control this same change removed.

The always-visible STOP button and the ESC hint are drawn on top of the radar. `.app.focused .bar > .play` is placed at margin 8px/10px, and `.app.focused .bar::after` (line 123) starts at margin-top:12px immediately to its right. project/plugins/radar.js:412-415 draws its filled rounded panel at left=16*unit, top=16*unit, size=190*unit with unit=clamp(height/720,0.7,2). At the viewport size this was verified against (764x485) unit is 0.7, so the radar box is (11,11)-(144,144) and the STOP button occupies roughly (10,8)-(56,30) — sitting on the radar's top-left corner and its rounded border. The 9.5px hint then runs horizontally from x~66 across the radar's face for nine seconds, and the animation restarts every time `.focused` is re-added, i.e. at the start of every single play. In Counter-Strike the top-left is the radar and nothing else; this is the corner a player glances at most. Technically correct, feels wrong.

focus() resizes the renderer but nothing repaints the four 2D overlay canvases, and in edit mode nothing ever will — so stopping play now leaves a stretched, wrong-scale ghost HUD over the restored editor. plugins/builtin/hud.js, project/plugins/{counter-strike-hud,radar,buy-menu}.js all paint from `phase:'frame'` systems, and engine/index.js:83 runs only renderer.sync/draw in edit mode (never the frame systems — this is recorded as painpoint p34). engine/loop.js:163 cancels the pending rAF, so there is no final clearing frame either. On stop the canvas elements shrink from the fullscreen size back to the editor viewport while their backing stores stay at the fullscreen size; the browser stretches the old bitmap into the new box, so the crosshair, radar and HUD are left frozen, squashed and at the wrong aspect over the editor's 3D view until you press play again. The ghost itself is pre-existing; the wrong scale and aspect are new, and they directly contradict "stopping gives the editor back exactly as it was". The spec told you to check every canvas layer against the viewport growing — nobody checked it shrinking.

`play.focus <anything-not-true>` silently means "off". `wanted === true || wanted === 'true'` turns `play.focus yes`, `play.focus 1`, `play.focus on` into applyFocus(context, false) with no complaint, so a mistyped argument un-focuses the game and reports focused:false as though that were what was asked for. Every other refusal in this file is named out loud; this one is not.

`test.is(realShell.focus(false), false, 'and it comes back')` is a tautology. engine/shell.js:51-61 returns `wanted` on the already-in-that-state path, `wanted` after toggling, and `false` when there is no frame — so focus(false) returns false for every possible input and state. The assertion cannot fail. (The `realShell.focused` check on the next line is the one doing real work.) Note also that this whole block is skipped where the tests actually run: headless has no context.shell, so shell.focus — the kernel primitive this task added — is exercised by no assertion in the suite. That part is disclosed honestly via test.note, but the summary's claim that the test "asserts the contributed panel set is byte-identical before and after" is hollow headless: with a stand-in shell nothing between `before` and the comparison can touch loader.contrib.panels.

The kernel table still says shell.js owns "four docks, a toolbar, a status line" and line 28 still counts it at 183 lines; it is now 216 and owns focus()/focused/root as well. The agent flagged this as deliberately not done because another agent holds the file, which is a reasonable call — but the kernel vocabulary table is the one place a plugin author looks to discover that shell.focus exists, so until it lands the primitive is undiscoverable except by reading shell.js. `node bin/engine.mjs check` does not catch this.

showInHand() has no `damageable.alive` check, so every corpse on the map is drawn holding a weapon. weapons.drop() (project/plugins/weapons.js:1087-1088) sets bag.current='' and then immediately re-selects slot 2 or 3, so a dead body's `current` is never empty. Verified live on de_dust2: killing terrorist-0 leaves damageable.alive=false, carriesWeapons.current='glock18', attachments.weaponMount='counter-strike/models/glock18.glb'. damage.js also flattens the collider but not the mesh, so the result is a sunken standing model with a pistol welded to its hand while the dropped-weapon event says the gun is on the floor. driveViewmodel (line 514) does check `alive`; this path does not, and the inconsistency is the tell.

NOT this agent's file, but it makes the whole of part two invisible in the shipped game. The level's camera block says "mode": "ortho". camera.js applyRule() copies rule.mode into view.mode on play:started, and render.js:1697 skips the viewmodel pass entirely whenever flat() (view.mode==='ortho'). Verified by driving a headless world: after editor.togglePlay() on de_dust2, view.mode==='ortho', and although state.shown is correctly {hands-counter-terrorist.glb + usp.glb}, draw() never renders it. Part one (weapons in everybody's hands) does draw. The mode was almost certainly written there by engine/start-world.js:244-245, which folds the editor's own view.mode back into the level on save.

driveViewmodel never consults context.view.mode, so it builds and pushes a viewmodel in ortho too. The frame system (line 396) then calls renderer.viewmodel.set(state.shown) every frame, which fetches and instantiates hands-*.glb plus the weapon GLB into a scene render.js:1697 will never draw. Two model loads and a live scene graph for a picture that cannot appear. It is also fragile in the other direction: render.js's flat() is only mode==='ortho', so any 3D camera that is not first person (a third-person follow) would get the hands and rifle pasted over the screen.

The sway is fed the recoil-included aim (aimOf, line 691), so a shot's own upward punch registers as a turn the gun must lag DOWN from, and it cancels part of the kick it is supposed to accompany. Measured live on the first AK shot: rotation.x = +0.02556 where the kick term alone is bag.kick(0.4431) * KICK_PITCH(0.07) = +0.03102 — 18% eaten; position.y = +0.00376 where the kick term alone is +0.00532 — 29% eaten. Between shots camera.decayRecoil reverses the sign, so a spray gets a counter-oscillation riding on the kick. The comment at line 548-550 argues for it deliberately, but the gun already follows the aim by virtue of being drawn in view space, so this term only subtracts from the one motion the brief said must read clearly.

`if (!wanted && !entity.attachments) return` is unreachable. When wanted is null, `held` is also null unless entity.attachments exists, and line 497 (`if (held === wanted) return`) has already returned for that case; when entity.attachments does exist the second condition is false. Dead line.

`&& id !== 'c4'` in the unmapped filter is dead — attachmentFor('c4') returns the C4 attachment, never null, so c4 can never reach that filter. Harmless, but it reads as though the bomb were an exception to the coverage check when it is not, and it invites the next reader to add real exclusions there.

The determinism assertions run one pure function twice over identical inputs inside the same loop and compare the two bags. Nothing in advanceViewmodel can make those diverge short of module-level mutable state or a random source being introduced later, so the check is close to a tautology. It is the honest headless stand-in for 'a replay bobs identically' and it does guard against a future regression, but it should not be read as evidence that the live lane replays identically — the fields feeding it (context.time, camera.aim(), velocityX/Z) are never exercised twice.
